answer: pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> sets the per-instance limits: add or set with low-threshold and high-threshold (uint64, int64 or decimal64, or na / not-supported; default na). direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all); location is all, na, near-end or far-end (default all). pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter> holds the per-type values and also shows default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value, e.g. set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200. The alert is armed with set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true; new resources inherit it from pm-profile-entry default-tca-supervision. show pm-parameter gives the exact parameter name and units.

Enable both switches: set ntp ntp-enabled true (default true) ntp-auth-enabled true (default false); assignment-method is manual, dhcp or both (default both). Add the key: add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <sha-1|aes-cmac|sha-256|md5> key-value <string 8..40> is-trusted true, key-id range 1..65534, is-trusted default false. Bind it: add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <key-id>, address being IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS name, origin manual or dhcp (default manual), admin-state unlock by default. Verify with show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>: auth-status (ok, yes, bad, none), reach (377 means all recent probes answered), stratum, when, poll, delay, offset, jitter, condition (sys.peer, reject, candidate). show ntp ntp-active-server names the server in use and show clock time-source should read ntp.

Traffic: protection-switch [-f] operation-type=<force|lockout|manual|release> switch-target=<value> protection-group=<value>, operational mode only; switch-target is not needed for release and lockout. Example: protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection. The persistent equivalent is protection-group pg-request (clear, manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout, exercise; default clear), with pg-state and last-switch-trigger showing the result. Controller: manual-switchover [-f] resource=<AID> switches the controller card role, e.g. manual-switchover card-1-3. It warns that the controller will switchover and the connection to the management interface will be lost, and needs confirmation unless -f is given.

set-time is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled, so with NTP running the manual set is rejected. Run show clock: time-source is ntp or manual (default manual), plus current-time, universal-time, timezone (default Universal-Time-Coordinated), uptime, DST-active and last-time-jump (jumps under 10 seconds are ignored). Then check show ntp (ntp-enabled, ntp-auth-enabled, ntp-active-server) and show ntp-server-status-<ip-address> for stratum, reach, offset, auth-status and condition. If manual time is really wanted, set ntp ntp-enabled false first, then set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z: ISO 8601 combined date and time, Z for UTC or +/-hh:mm for another zone. The time command prints the current time in the configured timezone.

show ne gives ne-id, ne-name (default 1830 GX), ne-type (G30, G40), node-type (ILA, OADM, XPDR), ne-site, ne-location, clli, node-controller-chassis-name and recover-mode. show chassis-<name> gives required-type (G31, G32, G34c, G42), is-node-controller, chassis-role and active-controller-slot. show slot lists each position with supported-type, installed-type and current-equipment; show card-<name> adds category, last-reboot-reason and last-reboot-time; show inventory gives serial-number, clei and part-number; uptime shows how long it has run. Then restart [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]: warm is the default and non service affecting, connectivity returning within five minutes; cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting; shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. With no resource-id the active controller is restarted, and confirmation is required unless -f is used.

slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>, here slot-1-2, is the equipment holder: show slot-1-2 gives supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment. The occupant is card-<name> (card-1-2) with required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, chassis-name, slot-name, subslot-name, category and subcard-list. Under the card sit port-<card-name>-<port-name> objects (port-type line, tributary, pluggable, comm, usb, ocm and others), and where the port is a cage the pluggable is tom-<card-name>-<port-name>, required-type CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP or SFPPLUS; its tributary port termination point is auto-created and auto-deleted with the TOM. Cards also expose sub-component-<card-name>/<sub-component-name>. FRU data for the pluggable comes from show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>, e.g. show inventory-1-3-1: hardware-version, actual-type, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, insertion-date and fw-status.

Capability objects are keyed by card-type, not by instance. show supported-card-<card-type>, e.g. show supported-card-CHM1R, gives node-type-compatibility (all, ILA, OADM), supported-subtype, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support (default general-c-band), max-power-draw, console-port-support, support-serdes-config and supported-bands (default standardC-band). show supported-slot-<card-type or chassis-type>/<slot-name> lists possible-card-types (max 15), configuration-mode (system-configured or user-configured) and requires-blank-when-empty; show supported-port and show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> cover ports and pluggables. What the fitted unit is doing comes from the instance, show card-1-7: required-type, card-mode, power-profile, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state.

The order is instance, area, interface. add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <dotted-quad> [version ospfv2|ospfv3, default ospfv2] [router-id-mode manual|use-loopback, default use-loopback]; instance-id is 0..255 and with use-loopback an ipv4 LO-MGMT address must already be configured. The instance must exist before add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> (ospf-area-type normal), and instance and area must both exist before add ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>, which references an existing interface: enable default true, hello-interval 10 s (1..32767), router-dead-interval 40 s (4..65535), retransmission-interval 5 s, transmit-delay 1 s, ospf-cost 10 (1..65535), priority 1 (0..255). Progress: show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<area-id>/<if-name>/<router-id>, state down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading, full, role dr, bdr, drother or ptp. The far end needs its own instance, area and interface, the NEs must be connected with DCN interface bridges, and the neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface goes down.

show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>, location-id being <chassis-id>-<slot-id> and swload-state active, inactive or installable, e.g. show software-load-1-5/active. It reports swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status (validate, apply, activate or cancel, each in-progress, complete, failed or timeout), swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), vendor, product, label and pkg-type. Individual pieces: show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> with state (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown), version and description, and show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> one level deeper. Bundled firmware: show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> fw-version, which can differ per equipment-type. show controller-card-<name> shows which controller is active or standby.

The per-port mode is lldp-admin-status on the ethernet, eth-zr or comm-eth facility: tx-only, rx-only, tx-and-rx or disabled, default disabled, e.g. set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx. Counters come from show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress: total-frames-out shows we are transmitting, total-frames-in that we are receiving, plus error-frames, total-discarded-frames, total-discarded-tlvs, total-unrecognized-tlvs, total-ageouts, last-change-time and last-clear-time (counters default 0). All counters freeze while lldp-admin-status is disabled for that port, and the egress direction is not supported. show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> shows what we advertise; show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/ingress shows the discovered far end with age and ttl, ttl falling back to the global lldp hold-on-timer, default 900 seconds.

show slot, addressed slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> or slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>, lists every position with AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment; a blank installed-type means no FRU is present. show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> gives the FRU data of what is fitted: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and insertion-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ or NA), number-of-lanes, actual-power-class (1..8), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status (not-applicable, current, not-current, unavailable). Firmware level: show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name>, giving fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status (current, not-current, unavailable; default unavailable).

show manifest lists the downloaded manifest files, and show manifest-<manifest-file> gives manifest-signature, downloaded-on and information. Contents: show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> reports each package's state (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown; default unknown), version and description, and show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> gives the bundled fw-version. show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type> shows the packaged FRU information for an equipment type and show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> lists the image files with their signature. For what is actually installed on the node, show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> and show sw-subcomponent-... report the same installed / not-installed / installation-failed / unknown state per piece.

Both come from per-resource-type profiles, and both containers are system managed and cannot be deleted manually. Alarms: set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>, direction na, ingress or egress and location na, near-end or far-end; show also returns service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). Example: set alarm-severity-entry-tom/EQPTCOMFAIL severity major. The container is alarm-severity-profile. PM: set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision <true|false> default-tca-supervision <true|false>, deciding whether newly created resources of that type get PM data supervision and threshold crossing supervision. Its container pm-profile has global-data-supervision auto-enabled or manual (default manual); with manual the flag is controlled per pm-profile-entry or per pm-control-entry.

ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> makes the decision: action is protect, bypass or discard, default protect. It also carries priority (uint8, mandatory on add, giving precedence between SPD entries), ipsec-protocol ESP, mode tunnel or transport (default tunnel), esn (default true), anti-replay-window 32..1024 default 64 when action is protect, and dynamic-ts (default disabled). Beneath each entry hang ipsec-traffic-selector-<instance>/<peer>/<spd-entry>/<selector-name> objects with next-layer-protocol (any = 0, opaque = 255, or 0..255; default any), and under each selector the local-subnet and remote-subnet prefixes plus local-ports and remote-ports ranges keyed <start>/<stop>, start being all, opaque or a port number and stop defaulting to 0, accepted only when start is all or opaque. The container is security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>.

trusted-certificate-<id> is the CA you trust: the X509v3 Root and Intermediate CA certificates trusted by the system. local-certificate-<id> is this node's own X.509v3 end-entity identity for the secure applications; it exposes trust-chain, used-by and self-signed. peer-certificate-<id> is the far end, the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application, and it uniquely has white-listed, true meaning it was white-listed at import with no trust chain. The fourth name is not an instance: show certificates lists all managed local, trusted and peer certificates imported as PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 bundles, show certificate-revocation lists revocations, and clear certificate removes one. All three instance objects share revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked; default auto), status, public-key-length (rsa2048 to ecdsa521), key-usage and extended-key-usage.

import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>], operational mode, e.g. import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=trusted-cert-1 <PEM string>. The -i flag also imports intermediates from a bundle or via the AIA extension; root certificates must be installed individually, and with no certificate-name the name is derived from the topmost issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix. Alternatively download filetype=trusted-certificate, local-certificate, peer-certificate or crl from an sftp or scp URL or a configured file-server, with passphrase and certificate-name. csr-gen creates a local-certificate in pending-import state and emits a PKCS#10 PEM CSR; cert-gen makes a self-signed certificate. Removal: clear [-f] certificate type=<trusted|local|peer> id=<id>, where the id must match an installed but unused certificate; type also accepts purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused.

access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name> decides permission: action is permit or deny and is mandatory at creation, filtering on path (XPath of a data node, notification, RPC or an external command), module-name (default *), attribute, attribute-value and operation (create, read, update, delete, execute; default *). access-rule-list-<name> groups them and controls evaluation order, being processed in order of sequence-id, lower ids first, with user-group naming which groups it applies to. These govern management and data-node access, not packet forwarding: packet filtering is acl-<name> (type IPv4 or IPv6, bound to an interface such as 1-AUX-1, DCN or DCN-B) with ace-<name>/<sequence-id> entries whose action is drop (default), accept or reject. sw-control-rule-<service-name> has nothing to do with traffic: it sets fail-action (default-action, ignore, system-restart) when a software service fails.

Evaluation is by sequence-id and lower numbered ids are processed first, both for access-rule entries within a list and for access-rule-list entries. If sequence-id is not supplied it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, so the new entry goes to the end of the list; the id can be changed later to re-sort entries. So of two matching rules the one reached first, the lower sequence-id in the earlier processed list, takes effect and its action (permit or deny) applies. The user-group leaf-list on access-rule-list accepts a maximum of 20 user-groups, with the default * matching all existing user-groups. Other stated limits: a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists, and the attribute and attribute-value leaf-lists take at most 10 entries of 64 characters each.

The trap community string is not part of snmp-community. The guide states that the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. Set it on the trap listener: add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [snmp-version v2c|v3, default v2c] [trap-community-string <string 0..32>, default infinera] [target-port <0..65535>, default 162] [target-transport udp] [enabled true], or change it later with set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value>. snmp-community-<name> only carries the polling community: community-string (1..32 characters), community-string-access read-only, enabled default true. Confirm with show snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string, and check show snmp enabled (default true) and port (default 161).

external-fiber-connection is the one written for you: the guide notes it is set autonomously by TNMS, and although manual configuration is possible it is not recommended. It represents the physical link between L0 ports in different NEs, or within one NE in disaggregated configurations: add external-fiber-connection-<name> src-port-name <value> dst-port-name <value> [src-node-id] [src-card-name] [dst-node-id] [dst-card-name] [scope general-purpose|cable-id, default general-purpose] [fiber-connection-type one-way|two-way, default two-way]; scope must be cable-id for the entry to take part in CableID path verification. By contrast fiber-connection-<name> is the intra-NE link between two ports or sub-ports of the same NE, which you add with src-port and dst-port. supporting-fiber-connection-<name> is read-only and just shows the fiber-connection-list supporting an entity.

Use ipv4-address: add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>, for example add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0' or add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0. Addresses beginning with 0, with 127, or with 224 through 255 are disallowed and only valid netmasks are accepted; show returns origin, static (default), dhcp or auto-config. The other two are read-only LLDP views, not configuration. management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports the management address advertised by the remote system seen on that port; management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports the one this system advertises. Both expose only if-subtype (unknown, if-index, system-port-number), if-id and address-oid, and each management address must have a distinct subtype and address.

The stated pre-condition on ipv4-address is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. Check interface-<if-name>: ipv4-address-assignment-method is static or dhcp (default static) and ipv4-enabled is true or false (default true). Put it back with set interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method static, then add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>. The address must also be legal: those beginning with 0, 127, or 224 through 255 are refused and only valid netmasks are allowed. To see which interfaces are available, press ? after ipv4-address- for the object completion options, or run show interface, which lists if-name, if-type (ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp, hdlc), supporting-port, backup-port, vrf, protection-mode, admin-state and oper-state.

show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> lists the system routes from all sources; source-protocol identifies where each came from, for example OSPF, BGP or static, and special-next-hop is none, blackhole or unreachable. The containers are rib-<rib-name>, with vrf and address-family ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast and one system-controlled default RIB per address family per routing instance, plus show routing for general information and show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> for the next-hop-address, e.g. show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN. Hand-typed routes go in with add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> next-hop-address <ip> [distance 1..255, default 1] [advertised true|false, default false] [interface] [special-next-hop blackhole], and ipv6-static-route for IPv6; origin is manual or dhcp.

local-ports and remote-ports belong to the IPsec/IKEv2 tunnel. Both are keyed <ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop> and give the local or remote Layer 4 port range of a traffic selector: start may be all, opaque or a port number, and stop defaults to 0, which is only accepted when start is all or opaque. Examples: add local-ports-ipsec/GX2/tacacs/ts1/all, add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53, add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/49/49. connection-ports is the connectivity one: show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> returns port-name, the dwdm-line port of an RD or ILAx card for that degree, and the OMS of that dwdm port is created as a consequence. degree-number ranges 1..20 and index is always 1 in the 1830 GX because dwdm-line ports are bidirectional.

take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>] makes the copy, storing the current Configuration database into one of the backup slots. db-instance is temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback, and description is up to 128 characters, e.g. take-snapshot manual description='Recover point'; taking one that already exists overwrites the existing file. activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override true|false, default false] puts it back, and a snapshot must have been taken before it can be activated. show database lists them, database-type active, manual, oneday, onehour, oneweek, rollback or temp, with database-state, backup-time and description. Refusal: the system only accepts take-snapshot if the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption is configured, globally via set security-policies db-passphrase or inline. It needs a minimum of 40 characters, no dictionary words, and special characters from the 85-character Z85 set.

activate is a multi-purpose operational-mode command. Its parameters are: activate-file; swimage (activates the currently installable image, implies a system restart, db-action auto|empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback, default auto, label picks the image); database (activates the currently inactive database, implies a restart, db-instance active|manual|oneday|onehour|oneweek|rollback|temp, db-passphrase 40..200 chars, restart-type cold|warm default cold, sanity-check-override default false); location-led (entity = chassis or card, led-mode flash|solid default flash, timeout 0..120 s default 0, only one test at a time); eqpt-fw (resource plus fw-image-name); krp (installs a Key Replacement Package); otdr and otdr-fiber-check; and loopback (WSS loopback on an NMC). -f skips the confirmation. For the database case there is also a separate command, activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override], whose pre-condition is that a snapshot must already have been taken with take-snapshot.

capabilities is per card: show capabilities-<name> retrieves the capability information of one card, the name being the card name. l0-capabilities is the photonic one: show l0-capabilities takes no parameters and shows the capabilities of the node's Layer 0 functions. oadm-capabilities is the add/drop one: show oadm-capabilities [max-degrees] [max-adgs] reports max-degrees (20, uint8) and max-adgs (110, uint8), the maximum number of Add/Drop Groups. Degrees and ADGs are only supported on OADM node types; for ILA the maximum degrees is 0 by convention and is not shown in supported capabilities. All three are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Note that per-card-type capability data, such as supported-features or support-serdes-config, lives in supported-card instead.

Use show controller-card-<name> for the controller only. It reports redundancy-status (active, standby, not-in-service; default not-in-service), redundancy-standby-status (ready-synchronized, not-ready-synchronizing, not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out, card-not-present), number-of-switchover-events, time-of-last-switchover (both only visible on the active controller) and additional-details (0..128 chars). For any card in the shelf use the card base object: show card-<name> with required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, category (line-card, fan, power-supply, other, carrier-card, blank), chassis-name, slot-name, power-profile, last-reboot-reason/time, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state. For what a card model supports use show supported-card-<card-type>: node-type-compatibility, supported-subtype, default/supported-card-mode, card-width, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, location-led-support, console-port-support, support-serdes-config, supported-bands, supported-features.

macsec-entity is the Ethernet MACsec object: add/set/show/delete macsec-entity-<name> with supporting-facility (an ethernet facility), enabled (default true), link-security-control must-secure|should-secure (default must-secure), replay-protection enable|disable, replay-protection-window 0..4294967295 (default 0), and the read-only negotiated-cipher-suite. The MACsec cipher terms are configured in mka-policy (macsec-cipher-suite, confidentiality-offset, key-server-priority, sak-rekey-interval 0|30..65535 s, default 30 s). secure-entity is the optical/L1 one: supporting-facility plus remote-secure-entity (remote optical-carrier on GX G40, remote ODU on GX G30, remote OTUFlex for CHM7/CHM7x), enabled default false, re-key-frequency 3600..86400 s default 28800, re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic|continue-traffic default continue-traffic, traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s default 0. Its cipher terms are read-only in secure-entity-sa-proposal: encryption-algorithm aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length key-length-256, integrity-algorithm none, dh-group ecp-521, proposal number 1.

They are two layers of the same ASE idler feature. ase-idler-service is the per-card service object (add/delete/set/show): function is idler, ase-idler-enable enabled|disabled (default disabled) turns on ASE filling of the unused and nmc-failed portions of the band spectrum, and the read-only ase-idler-state reports ase-enabled, ase-partially-enabled, ase-faulted or ase-disabled (default ase-disabled). ase-idler-source is the physical ASE pump (set/show only, no add/delete): function is ase-idler-source, pump-enable enabled|disabled (default disabled), read-only pump-state, target-output-power -3.00..20.50 dBm (default 13), plus admin-state, supporting-input-port and supporting-output-port. sw-service is unrelated: show sw-service-<sv-name> / show sw-services displays software services and containers running on the node (state off|ok|fail, cpu-usage, memory-usage, uptime, last-start-time, reboot-count).

No, both are disruptive. change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]enabled|disabled toggles Zero Touch Provisioning; change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, while change-ztp-mode disabled stops ZTP even if it is already in progress. The current setting is read with show ztp. clear [-f] recover-mode clears the recover-mode flag, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring traffic settings, so it may be traffic impacting; it takes no parameters. Both are Operational mode and prompt for confirmation unless -f is given. By contrast the carrier-mode objects are read-only: show golden-carrier-mode-<card-type>/<carrier-mode> and show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> only display capacity, client-mode, baud-rate, application, compatibility-id, status and supported-subtypes.

State: show third-party-app-<app-name> (also show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name>) gives version, vendor, product, label, state (running, stopped, failed; default stopped), information (0..1024 chars) and enable (true/false, default false). If enable is true the app is started and restarted on system restart; if false it is stopped, so set third-party-app-<name> enable false stops it. Firmware side: show third-party-fw-<fw-name> shows file-status (valid, invalid, missing), path, version, crc, vendor, part-number, nsa-upgrade-version and the present-in-eqpt / applicable-eqpt lists (max 80 elements each); those images are the ones used by activate eqpt-fw. To clear it: clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value> clears installed third party apps. To act on a running app without removing it, use appctl [app-name=] [command=] restart|netls|exec [target=] [parameters=], target defaulting to system.

Per-session is cli-session-config: set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value> sets the rows for that login only. cli-lines range 10..1000, default 40; cli-columns 80..4000, default 80; interactive-mode true/false (per session and not persistent); display-timestamp true/false, default false. The protocol as a whole is cli: set/show cli with enabled (default true, and it cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port (1..65535, default 22), script-dir, default-interactive-mode (default true, affects only new sessions) and show-alarm-columns (default default-columns), which has global effect on all CLI sessions. The two system configuration ones are config and configure: show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)] displays the non-default running configuration recursively from the current scope, and configure <exclusive|shared> [from-default | from-script=<value> | from-commit=<value>] enters Candidate Configuration mode, default target exclusive.

set is the generic attribute assignment: set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [...] [<filter>] changes attributes of existing managed entities, requires at least one attribute-value pair from the same entity, supports wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*), ranges/lists (card-1-[1..4]), and filters <attribute>=<value>; it prompts for confirmation when the request may be traffic impacting or implicitly affects multiple instances. set-alarm-state [state=] [[acknowledge-text=]] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]) is a separate alarm operation: state is mandatory (none, ack, close), alarm-id-list takes 1 to 10 alarm ids, acknowledge-text is optional (0..256 chars). set-time [new-time=]<value> is the time operation; it only applies when the time source is manual, i.e. NTP is not enabled, and the value is ISO 8601 combined date and time such as 2017-01-12T10:22:25Z or with +/-hh:mm. The one ending in -set is named-value-set, an object: add/set/delete/show named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value], value being a string 1..1024 characters.

mc is the Media Channel: add mc-<name> parent-oms <value> lower-frequency <value> upper-frequency <value>, all in MHz, with center-frequency and slot-width derived by the system, plus auto-delete (disabled by default, only allowed on RD66TM sleds with l0-mode-op=hsc-ols). nmc is the Network Media Channel, the actual channel carrying a service: add nmc-<name> parent-facility <value> center-frequency <value>, where parent-facility is either an MC or an OMS, center-frequency 190650000..196700000 MHz, width 15000..200000 MHz default 35000 (set to the 3 dB signal bandwidth matching the transponder baud rate), with input/output-attenuation-target 0..15 dB or max, power monitoring and the ASE insertion attributes. For both, the referenced supporting-card must be part of a Degree, not an ADG. mc-f and nmc-f are the read-only filler facilities that occupy unused spectrum: mc-f shows lower-frequency, upper-frequency and slot-width; nmc-f adds alloc- and actual- lower/upper frequency and bandwidth (alloc-bandwidth default 75000 MHz), power-actual-tx/rx and monitoring-state.

The scan is run by the activate command: activate otdr [entity=]<port AID> [[otdr-file-prefix=]] triggers a measurement on an OTDR port, and activate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<ots-r-id> runs a manual OTDR based fiber check; it errors out if a manual scan or an automatic Raman fiber check is already in progress, and if accepted it runs up to 3 OTDR tests with intermediate and final results. Tuning lives in otdr-ptp: otdr-range auto or 0..300.0 km, otdr-pulse-width auto or 10..20000 ns, otdr-measurement-speed fast|medium|slow|precision|auto|high-precision, otdr-ior auto or 1.0..2.0, otdr-fiber-type, otdr-resolution auto or 0.4..100.0, otdr-direction-mode default counter-prop-in-service, peak-power auto or 5..14.5, launching-fiber-length 0..50 m. Results come out of otdr-ptp (otdr-last-measurement, otdr-last-measurement-file, the generated .sor file, and otdr-fiber-break-distance in km, or not-available) and of otdr (otdr-state not-available|idle|measuring|finished|fail, otdr-error).

Origin decides it. On the dns instance, assignment-method is manual, dhcp or both, and the default is both, so the system accepts DHCP-supplied name servers; dns also has enabled (default true) and search. Each entry then carries its own origin in dns-server: add/set dns-server-<address> origin dhcp|manual, default manual. An entry with origin dhcp is one assigned by a DHCP server and will be re-learned; you can convert a DHCP-learned entry into a manual one by setting origin to manual, and clear dns [[target=]] clears entries. For the relay, the global object is dhcp-relay with mode disabled|ipv4|ipv6, default disabled, plus server-address (at least one IP address must be configured when enabled). The per-interface switch is if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true|false, default false, and it obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so a relay does nothing unless both the global mode and the interface flag are set.

clear [-f] system [type=] takes factory-reset, full-wipe or inactive. factory-reset resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing the respective files and user configurations; it does not take effect on GX G30 Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E) but is supported on the G30 FRCU, and the shutdown option is not supported on L0 cards. full-wipe cleans the entire system and reinstalls software on controller and line cards, removing all files, configurations and software, and needs a base software reinstall from ONIE to recover. inactive only clears the inactive software partition. target may be the whole system (the default) or a chassis/card AID, and restart-behavior is restart (default) or shutdown. The option that leaves logs and performance data behind is clear [-f] database (clear-type full, keep-networking or initialize-from-script, default full): it sets the NE database to default and reboots, but explicitly does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data.

Start with show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>, which lists inventory detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a multi-chassis configuration, with hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number and detection-timestamp. On the chassis object, show chassis-<name> gives is-node-controller, chassis-role (unknown, main-chassis, sub-chassis; default unknown), expected-serial-number, which is how the Node Controller is told a sub-chassis serial number, and equipment-discovery-ready, false until all equipment is discovered at startup. show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> gives the NCT topology with src/dst-chassis and src/dst-chassis-state of node controller, provisioned or unprovisioned. supported-chassis supported-subchassis-type lists accepted sub-chassis types (max 10; empty means no multi-chassis support).

control-mode on the amplifier object decides it: auto-max-pw (the default), where the system sets gain automatically targeting maximum output power, or manual, where you set it. amp-control-support reports whether auto is allowed at all (auto, or manual-only). In manual mode you use gain-target 0..40 dB (default 0.0) and gain-range-control is automatically set to manual with gain-range-target standard|low|high; in auto mode you can only bias it with gain-adjustment -20.00..20.00 dB (default 0, supported only on function pa or inline). Read-back values are gain-operating, gain-range-actual and control-state (unknown, not-applicable, stopped, converged, fine-tuning, adjusting). Things that stop output entirely: amplifier-enable disabled, which is the default, with output also depending on OSC presence for node-type ILA and on OMS facilities plus an existing OXcon for OADM; forced-shutdown true, used to shut down one amplifier on dual-band cards; admin-state lock; and an input OLOS shutdown after olos-shutdown-soak-timer 0..2000 ms, suppressible with olos-shutdown-disable true. gain-operating reads 0.0 when the card is out or the EDFA disabled.

Read the members with show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name>: state is active, standby, available or unknown, and role is working or protection, so the unit whose state is active is carrying traffic. At group level, show protection-group-<name> gives pg-state (no-request, forced/manual-to-working or -to-protection, sf-on-working, sf-on-protection, sd-on-working, sd-on-protection, wait-to-restore, protection-lockout, frozen, do-not-revert, unavailable, plus -remote variants for bidirectional SNCP), last-switch-trigger, remaining-wtr and switch-failure-reason. Behaviour is set by switching-mode unidirectional (default) or bidirectional, reversion-mode revertive or non-revertive (default non-revertive), hold-off-timer 0..10000 ms (default 0), wtr-timer 60..720 s (default 300, revertive only), and the triggers client-side-olos-trigger, client-side-sd-trigger, network-side-csf-trigger, network-side-sd-trigger, all disabled by default. Operator switching uses pg-request, pg-control-request freeze|clear-freeze, or protection-switch [-f] operation-type=force|lockout|manual|release.

Look at cable-id-path, which is the per port-pair result: show cable-id-path-<name> gives card-type-a and card-type-z (RD20TM or CAD10A, the only CableID capable sleds; the signal is passed transparently through the OPSM), port-a and port-z, port-a-to-port-z-path-status and the reverse (enabled/disabled optical continuity), port-a-to-port-z-last-test-status and the reverse (not-verified, pass, fail), current-state, last-test-qualifier (up-to-date or out-dated), last-test-timestamp and additional-info, which names the failure (Cable-ID TxLOS, Cable-ID RxLOS, Cable-ID-MISMATCH for misconnected fiber, Cable-ID-RxLOF, Power out-of-range, timeout). show -r adds the supporting fiber-connection list. To watch progress while it runs, use show cable-id-status: cable-id-state is idle, running-incl-switching or running-no-switching, and test-progress is a string of the form 'N out of M completed'. show cable-id lists all CableID entities and terminate cable-id stops all running verification tests; the feature itself is gated by equipment-policies cable-id-control (enabled by default only when l0-mode-op is slte).

aaa-server decides where authentication is sent: add/set aaa-server-<server-name> with protocol-supported RADIUS or TACACSPLUS (default RADIUS), server-address, server-priority 1..10 which orders the servers by precedence, enabled true/false (default true), role-supported (accounting, authentication, authorization; all three by default), shared-secret (max 64 characters, default sharedkey) and source-ip, the source IP used for RADIUS communications. Ports matter: server-port defaults to 49, server-port-authentication to 1812, server-port-accounting to 1813. What happens when it does not answer is governed by timeout, the Access-Request response timeout, 1..90 s, default 5, and retry, the number of Access-Request attempts to a single server before failing authentication, 0..5, default 1; total wait time, timeout x (retry + 1), must be under 5 minutes. For TACACS+ servers, show aaa-statistics-<server-name> counts connection-failures, which include unavailable servers and timeouts.

For the automation account use ssh-authorized-key: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label], where user-name is the local or remote user owning the key (0..32 chars), key-id is a unique name (1..64), and public-key is the OpenSSH/PEM encoded key up to 2048 characters; public-key-algorithm reads back as ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521 or ssh-rsa2048/3072/4096. That is the trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. For a remote host the node connects to, use ssh-known-host: add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label], address being the hostname, IPv4 or IPv6 address of the known peer, with ssh-ed25519 supported from R9.0. The node's own identity is ssh-host-key, one per supported algorithm, auto-generated in the default database and shown with show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm>; additional host keys are created or overwritten with ssh-keygen [-b=] [-l=] [-t=rsa|ecdsa|ed25519], default rsa.

The key agreement policy lives in mka-policy: add/set/show/delete mka-policy-<name> with key-server-priority, used by MKA to select the key server, macsec-cipher-suite for Secure Association Key derivation, confidentiality-offset, which is the number of octets in an Ethernet frame sent as unencrypted plain text, and sak-rekey-interval. The session key rollover is exactly that sak-rekey-interval, the Secure Association Key rekey interval in seconds, range 0|30..65535, default 30 s. The policy is bound to the port through macsec-mka-<name>: set macsec-mka-<name> mka-policy <name>, plus connectivity-association-key and connectivity-association-key-name (each 0..64 characters), psk-lifetime in days (1..173, default 14), psk-expiration-warning and psk-lifetime-enable, with is-key-server (default false) read back. Watch the channels on the read-only sc-tx and sc-rx objects: show sc-tx-<name>/<index> and show sc-rx-<name>/<index> give sci-tx or sci-rx as a 16-character hex string, state in-use or not-in-use as returned by the MKA stack, association-number, key-identifier and next-packet-number. macsec-entity itself reports the negotiated-cipher-suite.

NETCONF: set/show netconf, enabled default true, port 830 (1..65535, listens over ssh), hello-timeout 1..3600 s default 2, annotate-cli-name default false, static-info-in-notifs max 10 elements. It cannot be disabled from within a NETCONF session. gNMI/gRPC: set/show grpc, enabled default true, port 50051, gnmi-get-encoding-granularity per-path or per-object, default per-object. So both netconf and gnmi are on out of the box. The one that is partly off is RESTCONF: set/show restconf has enabled default true and https-enabled default true on https-port 8181, but http-enabled defaults to false (and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode) with http-port 8080; cookie-timeout is 1..300 minutes, default 5. For comparison, the CLI protocol object listens on port 22 and is enabled by default, while the ssh object, which is direct shell access on port 8022, is disabled by default (enabled false).

restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>] restarts a specific managed entity and requires confirmation unless -f is given. If you do not give a resource-id it restarts the active node controller card, and if you do not give a type it does a warm restart by default. The types are cold, which reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, with connectivity regained within five minutes; warm, which reboots only the processor of the card and is non service affecting, also regaining connectivity within five minutes; and shutdown, which gracefully shuts the card down. So restart card-1-4 is a warm, non-service-affecting reboot of that card's processor. No, you cannot assume uniform behaviour: not all cards support all restart types, and exceptions are called out, for example a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost, a warm reboot of XMM4 loses visibility for 3 minutes, while a cold reboot of CHM6 or UCM4 is service affecting. Cards support cold, warm and shutdown, card sub-components cold and warm, and a tom cold only; list sub-components with show card resources.

Three things must be in place. First the global flag: set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates enabled, which defaults to disabled; enabling it does not retroactively apply templates, they apply from that moment onward, and disabling it leaves existing serdes configuration untouched. Second a template keyed on the TOM part number: add serdes-template-<name> tom-part-number <value> (1..16 chars) [card-types-applicable] [ports-applicable], ports-applicable being 'all' by default or up to 20 port names such as T1, T10. Templates apply to all line cards that support serdes, so the card must report support-serdes-config true in supported-card. Third the values, one per entry: add serdes-template-entry-<template-name>/<entry-name> value <value>, for example RxAmplitude, RxEQ, TxEQ, RxPreCursor, TxEQAdaptive. Then a TOM with that part-number is configured automatically; swapping in a different part-number resets serdes and re-applies the new template if one exists. Manual serdes values are kept even if they deviate, and apply-template serdes-template [applicable-tom=<list>] forces re-application.

ots is the Optical Transport Section, the fibre span itself: fiber-type-tx/rx (default SSMF), fiber-length-tx/rx auto or 0..500.0 km, span-loss-transmit/receive 0..80 dB, span-loss-reference configured or measured (default measured), external-attenuation-tx/rx 0..30 dB, target-power-setting manual|auto|auto-plan (default auto) and laser-safety-mode OPLM or APSD. oms is the Optical Multiplex Section, the multiplexed band on that span: monitoring-mode (intrusive by default, not-monitored for ILA), grid-mode flexible by default or fixed-50G-96ch, fixed-100G-48ch, fixed-75G-64ch, fixed-75G-64ch-oif, fixed-50G-7100, fixed-150G-40ch, lower/upper-frequency defaulting to 191300000 and 196150000 MHz, and attenuation-control-mode-rx/tx. ops is the Optical Physical Section, the single physical add/drop or express port: role tributary, multi-carrier, general-purpose (default), ase-input or active-multi-carrier, input-psd-profile -30..-6 (default -6), port-expansion no or y-cable. osc carries the supervisory traffic: osc-mode OC3 (155 Mbit/s) or 1GE for HSC OLS, l0-comm-interface-type ipv4 or ipv6 for inter-NE communication, osc-control auto or manual, target-output-power -2.5..4.5 dBm, voa-attenuation-target-rx 0..30 dB (default 10). It is switched off via ots osc-less, default disabled.

The action is set per tributary port on the trib-ptp object, attribute tributary-disable-action, which indicates what the network element does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, either shutting off the laser or inserting a replacement signal. The default is laser-shut-off; the other values are none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais and send-nos (GX G30 only), and which are supported depends on the card and service type. Timing is tributary-disable-holdoff-timer, 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0, where 0 disables hold-off; it applies only when the TDA action is laser-turnoff, holding the optical signal until the timer expires before turning the laser off. Related attributes are near-end-tda (default disabled), tda-degrade-mode (BERSD-ODU triggering ALS, default disabled) and forward-defect-trigger (true by default), deciding whether a client forward defect such as LF or ODU-AIS flows through to the line side or triggers an egress TDA action. Example: set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off.

The high-order ODU is created by the system: the odu command notes that when a CHM6 has an OTU configured, 'show odu' tells you if the ODU exists, and the high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created. The stated pre-condition on odu is 'Super-channel must be added before Low Order ODUs can be added', so the super-channel comes first. You then create the low-order ODUs by hand: add odu-<name> odu-type <ODUCn|ODUCni|ODU4|ODU4i|ODUflexi|ODUflex|ODU0|ODU1|ODU2|ODU2e> parent-odu <HO-ODU> time-slots 1..80 trib-port-number 1. Line OTUs are also user added: add otu-1-5-L1-1-OTU4-1 parent flexo-group-1-5-L1-1 time-slots 1. The 'class' attribute reports high-order, low-order or mapped, and 'managed-by' (system|user, default system) says who created it; only user-created facilities can be user deleted.

Bit error rate testing is the bert command: bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=egress test-duration=10, then bert stop/get/delete test-id=TestX (test-id is mandatory for stop; it is system generated if omitted). Signal types: none, PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV, scrambled-idles (100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles, ODU4 uses PRBS31/PRBS31NONINV; monitoring also allows fec-frames for CarrierCTP). test-duration is 0 (indefinite, the default) or 10 seconds up to 1000 hours. A persistent test pattern is injected on odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> via test-signal-type (none default, PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV), test-signal-direction (ingress default, egress, both) and test-signal-monitoring (true/false, default false). Loopback is the 'loopback' attribute on otu, optical-carrier, ethernet, fc, oc, stm, interlaken: none (default), facility (towards facility side) or terminal (towards terminal side), with loopback-mode loopback or loopback-and-continue.

At each end you need the supporting facility already created and the far end identified: add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility <value> remote-secure-entity <value>. supporting-facility is the optical-carrier for 1830 GX G40, the ODU for 1830 GX G30, or the OTUflex for CHM7/CHM7x L1 service encryption; remote-secure-entity is the AID of the remote optical carrier, remote ODU or remote OTUflex. The secure entity is disabled by default, so set enabled true; alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited. Key policy: re-key-frequency 3600..86400 seconds (default 28800), re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic or continue-traffic (default continue-traffic), traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 seconds (default 0, only used with kill-traffic). Certificates must be in place first: the local X509v3 end-entity certificate (local-certificate) assigned to the secure-application through active-certificate-id, the trusted-certificate CA chain, and the far end peer-certificate, which is defined as the trusted remote peer certificate for the L1 encryption secure application. All are loaded with import-certificate in PEM format.

The telemetry object configures persistent and dynamic telemetry (set telemetry id <string>, show telemetry); it is system managed and cannot be manually deleted. To see what is subscribed use show subscriptions for the list, and show current-subscription-<subscription-name> for each configured subscription: related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc), session-protocol gnmi, encoding (json, bytes, proto, ascii, json-ietf; default json-ietf), transfer-mode (stream default, once, poll), updates-only (default false) and user-access. To see what each one is watching use show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>: subscription-path (1..520 chars), subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode (target-defined default, on-change, sample), sample-interval and heartbeat-interval in milliseconds (both default 0; for a target-defined stream the system raises sample-interval to 10 seconds and heartbeat-interval to 20 seconds), and suppress-redundant (default true).

The configuration database is encrypted at rest: show db-protection-scheme reports encryption-algorithm xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 in XTS mode, 64-byte block size), integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512 or none, integrity-status passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled, and mode encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which can be changed via the db-migrate RPC. Before you can take a copy, a db-passphrase must exist: the system only accepts take-snapshot if db-passphrase is configured globally as part of security-policies (set security-policies db-passphrase, string 40..200 characters) or supplied locally as take-snapshot db-passphrase=***. The passphrase needs a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain dictionary words, and allows special characters from the 85-character Z85 set; automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. take-snapshot then stores into db-instance temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback, with an optional description of 0..128 characters. Existing snapshots are listed with show database.

Start with show rib-<rib-name>: each RIB is identified by name, holds a single address-family (ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast) and reports the vrf it is bound to; the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per routing instance per supported address family, so the vrf leaf tells you which instance the prefix landed in. Then show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> shows whether the prefix actually made it into the table and from where: source-protocol (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) and special-next-hop, which is none for normal routes, or blackhole or unreachable, and for those two no next-hop is created under the route. Confirm forwarding detail with show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> next-hop-address, for example show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN, where interface is the outgoing interface reference. show vrf-<name> gives the instance type (mgmt or internal) and its chassis-name.

Password acceptance is governed by security-policies: strict-password-check (default true) enforces minimum length 8, at least one lower case letter, one upper case letter, one number and one symbol, and the user name cannot be part of the password (when disabled the minimum is 1 character); minimum-password-length is 1..200 with default 8; enforce-password-history-check (default true) blocks reuse of any of the previous 5 passwords, with password-history-size 1..200, default 5. These only affect newly defined passwords. Lockout is on the user object: max-invalid-login is the number of consecutive invalid attempts before suspension, range 0-255, default 5, and suspension-time is the suspension duration, 0-1440 minutes, default 5. show user-<name> reports user-status lockout and failed-logins; security-policies also has disable-user-lockout. To clear a stuck session, list sessions with show session and then kill-session <session-id>, where session-id is of the form <ip-address>:<port>, for example kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212; it cannot be your own session, use exit for that.

Local files: log-file keeps number-of-files log files, range 1..20 with default 10, rotating when max-file-size is reached, range 1..30 megabytes with default 30; the oldest files are discarded once the count exceeds number-of-files. source-facilities defaults to all, sensitive-data defaults to none for a regular log-file (and only for log-file-default-audit-dbg), and by default severity is informational and above. The default system log file cannot be edited or deleted. syslog defaults: remote-logging-switch true, source-address localhost, log-file-message-coalescence true, log-relay false, assignment-method both, niap-compliant-logging false, privacy-mode false. The single switch that turns off everything remote is set syslog remote-logging-switch false, which disables all remote logging destinations. Individual collectors (log-server) default to port 514, transport udp, message-format rfc5424, enabled true, origin manual.

What is raised now: show current-alarms gives number-of-alarms and last-changed, and show alarms / show alarm-<alarm-id> lists each with resource, AID, alarm-type, perceived-severity, reported-time, service-affecting, alarm-category, corrective-action and operator-state. Most alarms have automatic raise and clear criteria; only a small subset must be acknowledged and cleared by hand, and those are the alarm-inventory entries with can-be-cleared-by-user = true (show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true). Clear one with clear [-f] alarm <alarm-type> [resource=...], for example clear alarm DBRESTOREFAIL. This mechanism applies only to system-wide alarms not associated with a particular resource. Whether inhibiting reporting drops alarms already up is the system-wide switch set alarm-control arc-behavior: leave-alarms (the default) leaves current alarms raised when ARC is set to inhibit, clear-alarms clears them.

Use the Equipment dashboard: status equipment lists every chassis, the cards per chassis with their subtype and the toms per card, and for each shows temperature sensors and power values plus presence, oper-state and alarms, for example 'chassis-1 G42 (NC) temp 25C | power 2.1/4400 W' and 'card-1-1 XMM4 temp 25C'. Narrow it by passing the chassis id, for example status equipment 5; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so it is either all chassis or exactly one. For the raw sensor readings use show pm, whose real-time PM per resource reports temperature (C) for cards, FANCTRL and PEM, inlet-temperature (C) for the chassis, and fan-speed (percent) per fan, with instant, avg, min and max columns. The physical state is reflected by the LEDs: show leds and show led status list led-<location>/<name> with status not-available, off, green, flashing-green, yellow, flashing-yellow, amber, flashing-amber, red, flashing-red, cycling or cycling-with-off (cycling is used for lamp test).

The ots facility describes the line. span-loss-derived-rx and span-loss-derived-tx are the measured span loss based on OSC, range 0..99 dB, where 99 dB means OLOS, and they are only relevant when an OSC channel exists; they include losses external to the fiber. span-loss-transmit and span-loss-receive are the configured fibre losses, 0..80 dB (rx also allows 99), default 0, and span-loss-reference selects which source the system uses for target power calculation: measured (default) or configured. span-loss-alarm-threshold (0..80 dB, or 99, default 99) is set autonomously by the system, is persistent across reboots and can be forced to refresh with the update command in measured mode. span-loss-aging-margin-rx is 0.00..10.00 dB, default 1.0, and external-attenuation-tx/rx are 0..30 dB. The amplifier object shows the compensation: gain-operating versus gain-target (0..40 dB), gain-range-actual, gain-adjustment (-20.00..20.00 dB), control-mode auto-max-pw (default) or manual, span-loss-control enabled by default, tilt-actual and tilt-target, plus input-power-mon and output-power-mon.

The client TOM terminates on trib-ptp, the tributary client physical termination between the transceiver and the client protocol layer (service-type 100GBE, 400GBE, OTU4, 4x100GBE, OTU2, 10GBE, OC192, STM64 and so on). Above it sits the client protocol facility: ethernet (or fc, stm, otu for OTU4 transport). The xcon binds that to the line side, for example add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1; xcon reports network-mapping (the server layer, ODUCn, ODUCni, ODU4, ODU4i, ODUflexi and so on), payload-treatment (transport, switching, transport-without-fec, regen, regen-switching) and from-adaptation/to-adaptation. The low-order ODU rides in the high-order ODU/ODUCn, which is carried by the otu (added with parent flexo-group-<name>) over the flexo-group. That is the end of the digital domain: trib-ptp, ethernet, odu, otu and flexo are classed transport-layer1, while optical-carrier, super-channel, nmc and mc are optical-layer0. The handover is at the optical-carrier (frequency, tx-power, modulation-format, baud-rate) bound into a super-channel.

No, they are two different mechanisms. A counter crossing a limit is PM thresholding: add or set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> low-threshold <value> high-threshold <value>, where each is a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), na or not-supported, defaulting to na. The crossing is only reported if TCA supervision is on for that entry: set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true, or set it for a whole resource type with pm-profile-entry default-tca-supervision. System defaults and the allowed range come from show pm-threshold-profile-... (default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value, max-value). How loudly an existing fault is reported is alarm severity: set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>, for example set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor, or set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value>. Both alarm-severity objects are system managed and cannot be manually deleted.

Stop the object reporting with its alarm-report-control flag: set card-<name> alarm-report-control inhibited, values allowed or inhibited. Every facility carries the same attribute (odu, otu, ots, trib-ptp, optical-carrier, amplifier, and so on, where the default is allowed). You can also move the card to set card-<name> admin-state maintenance, since admin-state accepts lock, maintenance or unlock with unlock as default. What happens to alarms already raised is decided system-wide by alarm-control: set alarm-control arc-behavior leave-alarms, the default, leaves the current alarms in a raised mode when ARC is set to inhibit, while set alarm-control arc-behavior clear-alarms clears the current alarms at that point. The related alarm-soaking-behavior switch is automatic by default, with no-soak removing soaking time for the alarms specified in the FM profile.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. show secure-application-<id> returns type (server or client), status (enabled or disabled), active-certificate-id, which is the list of certificates assigned to it (string 0..128, and multiple may be given, for example set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY), and in-use, a leafref to active-certificate-id, which is the certificate actually presented to the far end. Assign with set secure-application-WebGUI active-certificate-id client. For mutual TLS set verify-client-cert to required (default disabled, meaning no client certificate is requested); the change only affects new TLS connections. Before it comes up, the local X509v3 end-entity certificate and its trusted-certificate CA chain must be imported, for example import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <PEM string> <passphrase>, and for L1 encryption also the far end peer-certificate. show local-certificate-<id> status should read valid rather than pending-import, expired, revoked, untrusted or future.

Pipe the show pm output through display: show pm <command flag> | display csv produces CSV data importable to a spreadsheet such as Excel; display xml and display json are also available. Restrict the data to the 15-minute bins with the period filter pm-15min (the NE stores pm-15min and pm-24h granularities, where bin 0 is the current data and bins 1 to n are history). Useful flags on show pm: -t for a single generic table, -n=<number-of-records> for the maximum records per chassis (default 1000), -s=<skip-records> to page through, -st=<timestamp> and -et=<timestamp> in the format 2021-02-01T10:00:00+01:00, -sbin=<number> and -ebin=<number> to bound the bins (by default bin 0 is first and all available bins are shown), and -i=<chassis-name> for one chassis. pm-filter values are AID, data-type, parameter, resource and resource-type. Use show pm <tab> for the full list of supported filters.

Look it up in the PM catalog: show pm-catalog <string>, where string is the catalog name. For example show pm-catalog parameter-undersized returns pm-parameter-undersized with units packets and type counter. The equivalent per-parameter view is show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type], for example show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds, and show pm-parameter on its own lists all PM parameters. type is either counter or gauge, and units come from the set na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors, MHz. Both commands are show only and are available in operational mode and candidate configuration mode.

Turn off real-time data supervision for that resource with pm-control: set pm-control <entity> data-supervision false, for example set pm-control pm-resource-card-1-1 data-supervision false. data-supervision is a true/false flag covering real-time data supervision for the resource and its default is true. show pm-control displays the configuration for all currently existing resources in the system that support PM data. The per-instance equivalent is set pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision false, also true/false with default true. Both commands are usable in operational mode and candidate configuration mode. Note this stops the collection; to also wipe what is already stored use clear pm real-time, optionally narrowed by resource, resource-type, period, direction, location or AID.

Yes. pm-control-entry is keyed exactly on resource, period, direction and location, so the target is pm-control-entry-<resource>/pm-15min/ingress/near-end: set pm-control-entry-<resource>/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true. direction accepts ingress, egress, all or na with a default of all, and location accepts all, na, near-end or far-end with a default of all. The same entry also carries data-supervision (true/false) for PM data collection. show pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> [supported-parameters] [data-supervision] [tca-supervision] additionally returns supported-parameters, the list of PM parameters that this resource type supports for that direction and location, with a maximum of 100 elements. A real instance looks like pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end. Available in operational mode and candidate configuration mode.

Use show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]. For example show pm-parameter pm-parameter-undersized prints units packets and type counter, and show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds does the same for that counter; show pm-parameter alone lists every PM parameter. The type attribute is either counter or gauge. The units attribute takes one of: na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors, MHz. The same two fields are reported by show pm-catalog <catalog-name>. Both commands are read-only and available in operational mode and candidate configuration mode.

Yes: set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled. The pm-profile object contains all resources that support PM data together with their related default configuration; it is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. global-data-supervision takes two values: auto-enabled, which globally enables the PM data-supervision flag without having to toggle it individually, and manual, the default, under which the data-supervision flag is instead controlled per resource type via pm-profile-entry or directly per instance via pm-control-entry. View the current setting with show pm-profile. The command is available in operational mode and candidate configuration mode.

Use pm-profile-entry, which holds the PM configuration per resource type: set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision true [default-tca-supervision true]. default-data-supervision determines, for newly created resources of that type, whether they have PM data supervision automatically enabled; default-tca-supervision does the same for threshold crossing supervision. Both are true or false. direction accepts ingress, egress, all or na with default all; location accepts all, na, near-end or far-end with default all; period is a PM period such as pm-15min or pm-24h. Read it back with show pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> [default-data-supervision] [default-tca-supervision]. If you want it on everywhere regardless of type, use set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled instead. Operational mode and candidate configuration mode.

Use show pm-resource-<resource> real-time-data-last-reset, for example show pm-resource-trib-ptp-1-7-T9. real-time-data-last-reset is a date-and-time giving the last real-time data reset for that resource; if the data was never reset, it is the date and time of the resource's creation. The same show also returns resource-type, AID (string of 1..64 characters) and real-time-supervision (true or false, default true), and lists the resource's pm-control-entry children, such as pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end and .../pm-24h/egress/near-end. Real-time counters are reset with clear pm real-time, which can be narrowed with resource, resource-type, period (pm-15min, pm-24h, pm-real-time), direction (all, egress, ingress), location (all, far-end, na, near-end) and AID. Available in operational mode and candidate configuration mode.

pm-threshold applies to one existing system resource instance: add pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/errored-seconds high-threshold <value>, then set, show or delete the same key. Both low-threshold and high-threshold accept a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), na, or not-supported, and each defaults to na. period is a PM period such as pm-15min or pm-24h; direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all; location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all; parameter is the PM parameter identifier, here errored-seconds. The per-resource-type equivalent, if you want it for a whole class of facilities, is pm-threshold-profile, for example set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200. For the crossing to be reported, tca-supervision must be true on the matching pm-control-entry. Operational mode and candidate configuration mode.

Use show pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter> [low-threshold] [high-threshold] [default-low-threshold] [default-high-threshold] [min-value] [max-value]. default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold are the system defined default values for that parameter, while min-value and max-value are the minimum and maximum for the parameter, that is the range you are allowed to configure. All four are show-only and each is a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), na, or not-supported. low-threshold and high-threshold are the configurable values, set with the matching set command, for example set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200. direction accepts ingress, egress, all or na with default all, and location accepts all, na, near-end or far-end with default all. Available in operational mode and candidate configuration mode.

Use the clock command. Set the zone with `set clock timezone <value>`, e.g. `set clock timezone Beijing-Chongqing-Hong_Kong-Urumqi[GMT+08:00]`. The timezone value list runs from International Date Line West[GMT-12:00] through Kiritimati[GMT+14:00]; the default is Universal-Time-Coordinated. To see the time source, use `show clock time-source`: it returns ntp (the NE synchronises via NTP) or manual (the NE uses its own internal clock). Default is manual. `show clock` also returns current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds, DST-active (true/false, default false) and last-time-jump (format '<time1> to <time2>', jumps under 10 seconds are ignored). If DNS is not properly configured, `show clock` can take up to 2 minutes to respond. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration.

Yes. `set ne node-type OADM` is allowed, and node-type can only be set/changed on the 1830 GX G34c chassis, which defaults to ILA. Values are ILA, OADM and XPDR (G31/G32 default OADM, G34c default ILA, G42 default XPDR). G34c support for OADM began with R7.0. Preconditions to set node-type OADM: no OMS monitoring-mode in the system may be 'ila-with-equalization' or 'not-monitored', i.e. no 'spectrum' (or 'ochm') objects may exist in OADM, and no direction-* may exist. Going the other way, to set node-type ILA: no OMS monitoring-mode on the dwdm-line ports may be 'intrusive' (no RD or PAx card can exist), and no degree, no oxcon and no nmc may exist. Note the G34c SLTE l0-mode-op is supported only when node-type is ILA.

`show ne-function`. It is a show-only command with no parameters, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, and it displays the NE generic functions in one list. On a 1830 GX G30 node the output lists the directions and amplifiers together, for example direction-1 through direction-8, then amplifier-raman-1-7, amplifier-1-1-A, amplifier-1-1-B, amplifier-1-3.1-drop, amplifier-1-5-A, amplifier-1-5-B, amplifier-2-1-A, amplifier-2-1-B, amplifier-2-3-A, amplifier-2-3-B, and finally ne-function itself.

Use the ntp command: `set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true`. ntp-enabled takes true/false and defaults to true; ntp-auth-enabled takes true/false and defaults to false, so authentication must be turned on explicitly. The ntp object is system managed and cannot be manually added or deleted. Also relevant is assignment-method (manual, dhcp, both; default both), which selects whether the system uses manually configured values, DHCP-supplied values, or both. `show ntp [ntp-enabled] [ntp-auth-enabled] [ntp-active-server] [assignment-method]` displays the settings plus the currently active NTP server. For authentication to work you also need keys via `add ntp-key-<key-id>` and the server association via `set ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <value>`. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration.

NTP authentication keys are managed with `add|set|show|delete ntp-key-<key-id>`. The key-type attribute is the hash algorithm used for NTP message digest computation and accepts sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 and md5; there is no default, so key-type is a mandatory argument on add. key-id is a number in the range 1..65534. key-value is a string of length 8..40. is-trusted marks the key as a trusted NTP key and takes true/false with a default of false. Example: `add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera`. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Bind a key to a server with `set ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <key-id>`.

Yes. The ntp-server origin attribute is exactly for this: it is the NTP address assignment method, with values dhcp (address assigned to the system by a DHCP server) and manual (manually configured), default manual. A user can convert a DHCP configured NTP entry into a manually configured one by changing this attribute, i.e. `set ntp-server-<ip-address> origin manual`. Other ntp-server attributes are auth-key-id (uint32 or not-applicable, default not-applicable), label (string 0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock) and alarm-report-control (allowed, inhibited; default allowed). ip-address may be IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS domain name. Use `delete ntp-server-<ip-address>` to remove the server instead. Note also `set ntp assignment-method` (manual, dhcp, both; default both) controls which configured values the system uses.

Use `show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>`, for example `show ntp-server-status-172.19.13.218`. The key field is reach: the reachability of the configured server, an 8-bit shift register with the most recent probe in the 2^0 position, where the value 377 means all recent probes have been answered. Supporting fields are when (seconds since the last packet was received), poll (polling interval in seconds), delay (path delay to the server in ms), offset (clock offset to the peer in ms), jitter (path jitter in ms), stratum of the remote peer, refid (reference clock type or address, string 1..32), type (local, unicast, multicast or broadcast), auth-status (ok, yes, bad, none; default none) and condition (e.g. sys.peer, reject, candidate). Show only; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

With `restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]`, type may be cold, warm or shutdown, and warm is the default when <type> is not provided. Cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting; the system regains connectivity within five minutes. A cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost, while a cold reboot of CHM6, UCM4, etc. is service affecting. Warm reboots only the processor of the CHM6, UCM4, etc. and is non service affecting, with connectivity back within five minutes; on XMM4 a warm reboot is non-service-affecting but visibility is lost for 3 minutes. Shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. Not all cards support all restart types; toms support cold only. If <resource-id> is omitted the active node controller card is restarted. The command asks for confirmation unless -f is given.

`set-time` is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled; if NTP is running the node takes its time from the server and manual setting is refused. Check with `show clock time-source` (values ntp or manual, default manual) and disable NTP with `set ntp ntp-enabled false` if you really need to set the clock by hand. Syntax is `set-time [new-time=]<value>`, with the value in a format derived from ISO 8601 combining date and time, e.g. `set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z` where 'Z' is UTC. A non-UTC timezone is allowed by giving +/-hh:mm instead of Z, e.g. `set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00`. Retrieve the current time with the `time` command, which reports it in the system configured timezone rather than the timezone used in the set-time command. Access mode: Operational Mode.

Yes: `status equipment`. The status command shows dashboard-type summary outputs; the Equipment dashboard summarises all equipment in the system with relevant details such as temperature sensors and power values. It lists the chassis, the cards per chassis with their subtype, the toms per card, and generic status per item: presence or absence, oper-state and alarms. Output uses symbols, a check for oper-state enabled / admin-state unlocked / no alarms, a cross for oper-state disabled, and a padlock for admin-state lock. Sample rows show entries such as temp 25 degC and power 2.1/4400 W. The default scope is the entire network element; for large NEs you can filter by giving a chassis id, e.g. `status equipment 5`. Only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so you get either all chassis or exactly one. Access mode: Operational mode.

Use `clear [-f] system [[action=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>]` with type factory-reset.
