The default is 1500; on the 1830 GX G40 the default is 1518 for the DCN, AUX, AUX2, OFEC-CC, Craft, CHM6 and UCM4 interface types. The parameter is available only when the mode is L3 (mode takes L1, L2 or L3 and defaults to L3). It can be given on add or set: `add -m comm-channel-<name> type <value> parent <value> [mtu <value>] [mode <value>]` or `set comm-channel-<name> [mtu <value>]`. Related L3-only attributes are mru (64..1500, default 1500), restart-timer (1..10 seconds, default 3) and max-failure (2..10, default 5).

LLDP is off by default: `lldp-admin-status` on comm-eth defaults to disabled, with values tx-only, rx-only, tx-and-rx and disabled; it cannot be modified if the mode is L1. Enable it per port, e.g. `set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx` or `set comm-eth-1-13-ETH4 lldp-admin-status tx-only`. lldp-transmit-interval is 1..16383 seconds, default 30. lldp-mgmt-addr-if selects which interface IP is advertised as the management address (1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-2 (G30 only), 1-AUX-1-B, 1-AUX-2-B, DCN-B, DCN-2-B (G30 only), L0-MGMT); it applies when lldp-admin-status is tx-only or tx-and-rx and is empty by default, in which case the loopback IP is used, else the DCN/AUX IP, and if neither has an address the TLV is not sent. For speed, `auto-negotiation` defaults to enabled; rate (1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 Mbits or maximum, default maximum), duplex-mode (default full) and flow-control (default disabled) are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled. mtu is 1280..1500, default 1500.

Use `set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>]` and read it back with `show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]`, both available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. `mode` is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation and takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6, defaulting to disabled. `server-address` holds the DHCP server IP addresses as an IPv4 or IPv6 server address; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Examples: `set dhcp-relay mode ipv4` and `set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3`. These are the global settings; individual interfaces still have to opt in with `set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true`, which obeys the global dhcp-relay settings.

Yes. The dns object has an `assignment-method` attribute indicating whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values; it takes manual, dhcp or both, and the default is both, so out of the box the node accepts DNS servers from DHCP as well as manually configured ones. Syntax: `set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>]` and `show dns [assignment-method] [enabled] [search]`, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. `enabled` is the flag indicating if DNS is enabled, true or false, default true. `search` is the DNS-search-suffix name, a string of length 0..64 that must contain at least a single dot; to clear it, set the string to an empty string. Individual servers carry their own `origin` (dhcp or manual) on the dns-server object.

Add a name server with `add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>]`, where address is an IPv4 or IPv6 address; remove one with `delete dns-server-<address>`, and view them with `show dns-server-<address> [origin]`. The `origin` attribute is the DNS address assignment method and tells you where an entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that has been assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the DNS address has been manually configured. The default is manual. You can also convert a DHCP-configured DNS entry into a manually configured one simply by changing this attribute with `set dns-server-<address> origin manual`. Example from the guide: `add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp`. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the if-dhcp-relay object, which is keyed by interface: `set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>]`, and check it with `show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]`. `dhcp-relay-enabled` enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface and takes true or false, defaulting to false; it obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global `set dhcp-relay mode ipv4|ipv6` and server-address must also be in place. if-name is the interface object identifier, a string of length 0..255. Examples: `set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true` and `show if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled`. Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

By default a new interface is static and protected. On `add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> [if-description <value>] [protection-mode <value>] [ipv4-enabled <value>] [ipv4-address-assignment-method <value>] [ipv6-enabled <value>] [ipv6-address-assignment-method <value>] [proxy-arp-enabled <value>] [admin-state <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]`, both ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method take static or dhcp and default to static, and ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled are true by default. protection-mode takes unknown, protected or unprotected and defaults to protected, while the read-only protection-state defaults to unknown. proxy-arp-enabled defaults to false and is only applicable to the DCN interface. admin-state defaults to unlock, oper-state defaults to disabled, alarm-report-control defaults to allowed. if-type values are ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp and hdlc. Example: `set interface-DCN protection-mode protected`.

Yes, with an ip-monitoring instance, which periodically pings destinations and takes action on configured static-routes. Syntax: `add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]`. The `action` taken when the monitoring goes into 'failed' state is none or withdraw, and the default is withdraw, so the route is pulled automatically. `destination` is the remote host to monitor (IPv4 or IPv6). `next-hop` defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address, and the monitoring instance will not be active until the exit interface is configured. `probe-interval` is the time between two consecutive pings, 0...60 seconds, default 5. `drop-rate` is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1. `enabled` is true by default. `static-route` is the list of connected static routes, maximum 10 elements. The routes themselves report monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use `add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>`, for example `add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0'` or `add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0`. View with `show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin]` and remove with `delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>`. Pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. Only valid netmasks are allowed. The following addresses are disallowed: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), addresses beginning with 127 (loopback), and addresses beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). if-name is a string 0..64 characters; use ? after `ipv4-address-` to list the available interfaces. `origin` is show-only and reports static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The `distance` parameter on ipv4-static-route is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255 with a default of 1. To create a discard route, set `special-next-hop` to blackhole (blackhole is the only value, and it is also the listed default). Blackhole static routes are needed for routes that are not present in the IGP tables but must be advertised to an external AS, since routes advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, not by BGP itself. Syntax: `add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]`. `advertised` defaults to false; when true the route is advertised in the routing protocol, and for OSPF it is advertised as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR. `origin` is manual or dhcp, default manual. Example: `add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165`.

Almost, but the subnet is given as a prefix length rather than a netmask: `add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>`, with `show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin]` and `delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>`. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. Note that an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. `origin` is show-only and reports static, dhcp or auto-config, with default static. Use ? after `ipv6-address-` to list the available interfaces. Examples: `add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10` and `add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64`. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. The ipv6-static-route command takes an `interface` parameter, and the guide notes that static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Syntax: `add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]`. The VRF bound to the chosen interface needs to match the vrf provided on the static route. Example: `add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B`, alongside the DCN form `add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN`. distance is 1..255, default 1; advertised defaults to false; origin is manual or dhcp, default manual; special-next-hop is blackhole.

Use the management-address command, which retrieves management address information about a particular chassis component received from the remote system: `show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]`. lldp-port is the local port connected to this LLDP neighbor (an instance reference) and direction is ingress or egress. address-subtype is the type of management address identifier encoding used in the associated address attribute, and address is the string value identifying the management address component of the remote system, whose purpose is to contact the management entity, string length 0..64. if-subtype describes the basis of the interface type associated with the management address and takes unknown, if-index or system-port-number. if-id is the integer interface number for that management address on the remote system. address-oid is the Object Identifier used to identify the type of hardware component or protocol entity associated with the address advertised by the remote system agent, string length 0..128. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

They are the same set of attributes read from the two ends of the LLDP exchange, and they differ in their AID. management-address is keyed with a direction: `show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]`, where direction is ingress or egress. management-address-local has no direction component: `show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]`, and `show management-address-local` on its own views the management address information from the local LLDP ports. Both carry address (string 0..64), address-subtype, if-subtype (unknown, if-index, system-port-number), if-id (integer) and address-oid (string 0..128); on management-address-local the guide notes address-oid is currently an empty string. Each management address must have a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). Both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, the networking object has a `use-as-source` attribute: the interface to use as the source address. Syntax: `set networking [use-as-source <value>]` and `show networking [use-as-source]`, both available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The value is a string of length 0..64, naming the interface; no default is given. Example from the guide: `set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT`, and `show networking` to view the current networking information. This is the only parameter on the networking command.

Use `show networking-services`. This command is used to show the list of network services and takes no parameters at all; the whole syntax is just `show networking-services`. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. It is separate from the `networking` command, which only carries the `use-as-source` attribute naming the interface to use as source address.

Because the next-hop model is anchored on the RIB. Each next-hop entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. So the AID is show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address], where rib-name is a String of length 1..64 with pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 -.,]*), destination-prefix is an IP prefix, interface is the outgoing interface name (for example DCN), and next-hop-address is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Example: show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use clear ospf. Syntax: clear [-f] ospf [instance=]<value>. It removes and restarts an ospf-instance, and the operation is asynchronous, so the CLI does not wait for the restart to complete. The instance id of the ospf-instance must be provided as <instance> (type string). The -f flag forces the command without confirmation; without it you are prompted to confirm. Access mode is Operational Mode only. Example: clear ospf 1. The ospf-instance command description also points here for clearing an OSPF instance from the configuration asynchronously.

No. The ospf-area command exposes ospf-area-type, but the only permitted value is normal, and normal is also the default, so stub and NSSA area types cannot be configured. Commands are: add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type <value>], plus set, show and delete on the same AID. instance-id is uint8 in range 0..255 and ospf-area-id is a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ospf-area-1/0.0.0.0.

Use ospf-area-range, which summarizes routes for an OSPF area matching address/mask. It is applicable to Area Border Routers (ABRs) only. Syntax: add ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix> [advertise <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms. prefix is an IPv4 prefix (length <= 32) or IPv6 prefix (length <= 128) in canonical form; advertise takes true or false and defaults to true (true advertises the summary, false hides it). Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Example: add ospf-area-range-1/9.9.9.9/10.220.0.0/16 advertise true. Delete prompts for confirmation.

Yes. On ospf-instance the version parameter accepts ospfv2 or ospfv3, defaulting to ospfv2, and version is settable only at add time (add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <value> [version <value>] [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>]); set does not include version. The router id comes from router-id-mode, which is manual or use-loopback with default use-loopback. With manual you supply router-id as a dotted-quad; with use-loopback the ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured as a pre-condition. instance-id is uint8 0..255, description is a String of length 0..128. Example: add ospf-instance-2 description xyz router-id-mode use-loopback version ospfv3.

On ospf-interface the defaults are hello-interval 10 seconds (uint16, range 1..32767) and router-dead-interval 40 seconds (uint16, range 4..65535). Other timers: retransmission-interval default 5 (range 2..3600 s) and transmit-delay default 1 (range 1..450 s). ospf-cost defaults to 10 (range 1..65535) and priority to 1 (uint8 0..255, 0 means not eligible for DR/BDR). Authentication is available: ospf-auth-enable is true/false, default false; ospf-auth-algorithm is none or HMAC_SHA_256, default HMAC_SHA_256 and only relevant for ospfv2; ospf-auth-key is an ASCII string 0..256, also ospfv2 only. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance and OSPF area must exist before adding the interface.

Use show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id> [state] [role] [address] [priority] (Operational Mode). The state values are: down (initial, no Hello packets received), init (Hellos received but bidirectional communication not yet established), 2-way (bidirectional established, DR/BDR election occurs here), exstart (DR and BDR elected, master-slave relation determined), exchange (neighbors exchange DataBaseDescriptor packets containing LSA headers), loading (routers exchange full Link State information based on DBDs), and full (full adjacency achieved). Roles are drother (Designated Router Other), dr, bdr (Backup Designated Router) and ptp (point-to-point). Note an OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

Use ospfv3-ipsec-security-association: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> integrity-algorithm <value> [ipsec-protocol <value>] [ipsec-mode <value>], with set, show and delete forms. spi is a unique uint32 in range 256..4294967295. integrity-algorithm is mandatory on add and accepts AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256, AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 and AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96. ipsec-protocol supports ESP only (default ESP) and ipsec-mode supports transport only (default transport). Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 integrity-algorithm AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128.

Use ping [-c=<count>] [-w=<timeout>] [-s=<pktsize>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <ping-dest>. -i=<interface> specifies the source interface; by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF; by default the MGMT VRF is used. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. -c stops after sending count ECHO_REQUEST packets, -w sets a timeout in seconds after which ping exits regardless of packets sent or received, and -s sets the payload octets excluding headers, default 56 plus 8 octets of ICMP header for a total of 64. ping-dest may be an ipv4-address, ipv6-address or domain-name. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use show protocols, which lists all protocol information in one place. Syntax: show protocols [ssh|cli|serial-console|netconf|grpc|snmp|restconf|http-file-server|data-model-openconfig]. Bare show protocols lists ssh, cli, serial-console, netconf, restconf, grpc, snmp, http-file-server and data-model-openconfig; adding a keyword shows that protocol's detail, for example ssh with its host keys, enabled flag, port 8022 and pre/post-login messages; cli enabled true on port 22 with script-dir /storage/scripts; netconf enabled true port 830; restconf https-enabled true, http-port 8080, https-port 8181, cookie-timeout 5 minutes, api-root /restconf; grpc port 50051; snmp port 161; http-file-server http-port 8980, https-port 8981, url-base /transfer; serial-console global-timeout 60 minutes. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]. Each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB for each supported address family. rib-name is a String of length 1..64, vrf is a leafref to ../../vrf/name giving the VRF the RIB is bound to, and address-family takes ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast. Example: show rib-IPv4 views the RIB identified by the 'IPv4' key. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the route command, which shows the list of system routes from various sources such as dynamic protocols and static route. Syntax: show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]. The source-protocol attribute gives the source protocol for the route entry, for example OSPF, BGP, static. rib-name is a String of length 1..64 and destination-prefix is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. special-next-hop indicates the special next hop used for IPv4/IPv6 static routes, rib:routes and IP Monitoring, with values none (default, normal routes), blackhole and unreachable; for blackhole and unreachable routes no next-hop is created under the route. Example: show route. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. show routing displays routing information. It takes no parameters at all, so the syntax is simply show routing. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the detail behind it use the related commands: show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family] for the per-address-family RIBs, show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol] for the individual routes and their source protocol, show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address] for next hops, and show vrf-<name> for the routing instances.

supporting-interface shows supporting interface information, that is, the underlying IPv4/IPv6 interface that an interface is built on. Syntax: show supporting-interface-<name>/<interface>. name is the name of the interface (string). interface is a reference to the IPv4/IPv6 interface, given as a path pointing to ../../../../../networking/interface/if-name, so it resolves to an if-name under networking/interface. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

By default traceroute probes a maximum of 30 hops and uses the MGMT VRF. Syntax: traceroute [-m=<hopcnt>] [-w=<timeout>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <tr-dest> [pktsize]. -m sets the maximum hops (max time-to-live), uint8 range 1..255, default 30. -w sets the timeout in seconds, uint16 range 1..10, default 2. -v=<vrf> selects the VRF and defaults to MGMT if not provided; -i=<interface> selects the source interface, which by default is chosen according to the routing table. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. pktsize is the total probe packet size, uint16, default 60 (60 bytes for IPv4). tr-dest may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or domain-name.

Use show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description], which shows the Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instance. name is a String of length 0..32. type gives the VRF type with values mgmt (Management VRF) and internal (Internal VRF). chassis-name gives the associated chassis name for that VRF, which tells you which chassis it belongs to. description is a String of length 0..255 describing the VRF and its intended purpose. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: show vrf-MGMT displays the Management VRF attributes.

A successful swimage activation implies a system restart. Syntax: activate [-f] swimage [label <string>] [db-action <empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback|auto>]. The optional db-action specifies what happens to the database: auto (default) activates the image processing the database with the system default behavior, empty-db activates with an empty database, upgrade-db activates by upgrading the current database, and rollback rolls back to the previous active software image. If db-action is not provided the system decides automatically. Unless -f is given, the user must confirm the activation when prompted; -v forces the validate check again. label specifies the sw image/manifest file name, and if not specified the currently installable image is used. Access mode is Operational Mode.

No, only a single location led test can be running at a time. Syntax: activate location-led [entity=]<value> [[timeout=]<value>] [[led-mode=]<value>], where entity is a chassis or a card. led-mode is flash (default, amber light blinking at 1Hz, used for LED location) or solid (steady amber, used for lamp test, which lights all chassis LEDs amber). To turn it off use terminate location-led [entity=]<value>, or set timeout, a timer in the range 0..120 seconds; the default 0 means no timeout so the function runs until terminated. Note the timeout parameter does not take effect in 1830 GX G30 R5.1, so use terminate there. Not all cards support the Location LED test.

Use the bootstrap command, which establishes a TLS connection over the OSC link and provisions the initial administrator account on a neighbor NE that has no configured users yet. Syntax: bootstrap ([local-port=]<value> | [neighbor-address=]<value>) [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-password=]<value>. Select the neighbor either by local-port, the supporting-port of a MGMT vrf osc-eth interface as shown in show interface (for example 1-1-dwdm-line1), which the system maps to the OCE-<chassis>-<slot>-<vlan-id> netdev and resolves to the peer address with get_osc_neighbors.sh (the RPC is rejected if resolution fails), or by neighbor-address, the IPv6 link-local address of the OSC peer including zone (string 7..256, pattern 'fe80:.*'). new-admin-user is mandatory, length 1..32, following local user naming rules. new-password can be a SHA512 hash ($6$salt$hash, salt 2..16 chars) or plain text subject to system password complexity rules.

Type cancel-upgrade. The full syntax is cancel-upgrade [-h], where -h just displays help for the command; there are no other parameters. It cancels any active upgrade in progress. Access mode is Operational mode. Pre-condition: an upgrade must be in progress for this command to execute successfully.

change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, so on an in-service node you lose the configuration and the node reboots. Syntax: change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<value> with ztp-mode values enabled or disabled; -f forces the command without confirmation, so without it you are prompted. change-ztp-mode disabled disables ZTP and stops ZTP if it is already in progress; the command can be executed while ZTP is running, interrupting it. The current ZTP mode configuration is displayed with show ztp. Access mode is Operational mode.

Use show current-fw, which lists the current firmware available in the cards, with per-entry fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status. fw-status values are current (current firmware is up-to-date), not-current (current firmware is not up-to-date against the expected one) and unavailable (firmware status information is currently unavailable, which is also the default). AID forms are show current-fw-<card-name>-<port-name>/<fw-name>, show current-fw-<card-name>.<slot-name>/<fw-name>, show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name> and show current-fw-<name>/<fw-name>, each optionally with [fw-version] [expected-fw-version] [fw-status]. fw-name is a String of length 0..32. Example: show current-fw-1-3/DCO_1. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

download supports filetype values crl (CRL file in PEM format), database (a previously uploaded database), file (any file to the file-system), krp (key replacement package), local-certificate (PKCS#12 with password-protected private key, or PKCS#7 if pending-import), peer-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#12), script (a CLI script), swimage (downloads a manifest then all files of a SW image) and trusted-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#7 Root or Intermediate CA). The system automatically stores the downloaded file in an appropriate place; you do not provide a local location. The exception is filetype=file, where destination can be omitted (default directory, original name), a file-name only, a relative path or an absolute path, and you need write access to it; use show transfer to see the default storage directory. A downloaded database is stored as a db-instance=temp database, overwriting any existing temp.

Use show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature], which retrieves information about downloaded image files. manifest-file is the downloaded manifest file and its information (String, length 0..256), name is the name of the downloaded software image (String, length 0..256), and signature is the downloaded software image file signature (String, length 0..1024). Running show downloaded-image with no AID lists all the downloaded software image files. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

show downloads. It shows a list of downloads and takes no parameters. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands: show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature] retrieves information about downloaded image files including their signature, and show transfer-status is used to follow the progress of an asynchronous download started with download -a.

Not any file. The `file` command performs basic file and directory operations, but file system access is restricted to the current user's access, so not all files/directories are editable. Syntax: `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>`, Operational mode. Supported operations are rename (renames a file or directory), delete (deletes a file), view (listing for a file or directory), sha256sum (SHA256 hash checksum) and md5sum (md5 hash checksum). `new-file-path` is only used when the operation is rename, and its string pattern is '[A-Za-z0-9 \-/\.]*'. A `result` attribute reports the file operation result. Examples: `file rename /tmp/a.log /tmp/b.log`, `file delete /tmp/a.log`, `file view /tmp`.

Both are documented as performing basic file and directory operations in Operational mode, but `file` is the fuller command. `file-operation [[operation=]<value>] [new-file-path=]<value> [file-path=]<value>` supports only three operations: rename, delete and view. `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>` supports five: rename, delete, view, sha256sum (SHA256 hash checksum of a file) and md5sum (md5 hash checksum). `file` also has a `result` attribute for the operation result, is used by `show file <filename>` to display file contents, and pairs with `clear [-f] file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value>` to remove a krp, script or swimage.

Use `add file-server-<name> server-address <value> protocol <value> [server-port <value>] [user-name <value>] [password <value>] [initial-path <value>] [label <value>]`; also set/show/delete, Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `protocol` accepts file, ftp, sftp, scp, http, https. `file` represents local storage including USB and requires initial-path to be provided; ftp and http are applicable only when secure-mode is set to false. `name` is a String 0..64 characters, `server-address` is an IPv4, IPv6 or domain name, `user-name` 0..64, `password` 0..128, `initial-path` 0..256, `label` 0..256. `server-port` is a Number; if not provided, the default for the selected protocol is used. Example: `add file-server-139 server-address '10.220.227.139' protocol 'scp' user-name 'root' password 'Nokia' initial-path '/root'`.

Use `show filetype-<name> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [last-operation]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `name` is the file type for which the transfer happened. `last-completion-status` is the last transfer status (string), `last-transfer` is the last transfer start timestamp as a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ (see the set-time command), `last-duration` is the last transfer duration as a time-interval, and `last-operation` is the last transfer operation with values unknown, upload or download. Note that transfer status only exists if at least one operation of that kind was done for the specified filetype.

Yes, but HTTP is off by default. Use `set http-file-server [enabled <value>] [http-enabled <value>] [https-enabled <value>] [http-port <value>] [https-port <value>]` and `show http-file-server [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [url-base]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `enabled` (true/false) enables file server access overall and defaults to true. `http-enabled` defaults to false; `https-enabled` defaults to true. `http-port` is a Number defaulting to 8980 and `https-port` defaults to 8981. `url-base` is a show-only String of length 1..100 characters, default /transfer, the base URL used to redirect to the file transfer application.

Use the manifest commands, Operational and Candidate Configuration mode: `show manifest-<manifest-file> [manifest-signature] [downloaded-on] [information]` for the file itself, `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description]` for each package, and `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` for firmware. `state` values are installed (software package installed), not-installed, installation-failed (install failed) and unknown, with default unknown. manifest-file is a String 0..256, equipment-type 0..32, name 1..256, fw-name 0..32, manifest-signature a hex-string 0..1024, version 0..64, description 0..512, and downloaded-on a timestamp YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ.

No. Versions for the same firmware can be different per equipment-type within one software-load. Use `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` or `show packaged-fw-<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `location-id` is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> of the SW load subcomponent, a string of 0..64 characters. `swload-state` is active, inactive or installable. `equipment-type` is the type of equipment (card, etc) that will use this firmware, 0..32 characters, and `fw-name` and `fw-version` are also 0..32 characters. `show packaged-fw` lists all components' firmware versions in the load.

Yes. `prepare-upgrade` has two options: validate, which validates the software label/manifest, and apply, which applies it. Syntax: `prepare-upgrade [-f] [-i] [-u] [option=]<value> [manifest=]<value> [[db-action=]<value>] [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>`, Operational mode. Flags: -h help, -i ignore validation failures, -u unattended (auto-activate software after prepare-upgrade apply), -f force without confirmation. `db-action` (valid for unattended upgrade only) is empty-db, upgrade-db or rollback, default upgrade-db. `clear-type` is full (default), keep-networking or initialize-from-script. Example: `prepare-upgrade validate <label>` then `prepare-upgrade apply <label>`.

`clear recover-mode` clears the recover-mode flag. This action clears the current recover-mode state of the NE, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring the traffic settings. As such, it may be traffic impacting. The command has no parameters. Syntax: `clear [-f] recover-mode`, Operational mode. The only flag is -f, which forces the command without confirmation, so `clear recover-mode` prompts for confirmation while `clear -f recover-mode` runs without a confirmation prompt.

Use `show software-load-<swload-state>` or `show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>`, Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `swload-state` is active (active software load), inactive, or installable. Attributes: swload-version (0..64), swload-manifest (0..256, only relevant for installable), swload-prepared (true/false, only relevant for installable), swload-status, swload-information (0..1024), swload-activation-type, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label, swload-pkg-type. swload-status values include status-unknown, validate/apply/activate/cancel -in-progress, -complete, -failed and -timeout. swload-activation-type (installable only) is direct, warmstart or coldstart. Example: `show software-load-active`, `show software-load-1-5/active`.

Use `show software-location-<location-id>`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `location-id` is the location of the equipment, a String of length 0..64. For example, `show software-location-1-5` retrieves software location information from the card in chassis 1, slot 5. The same slot view is reachable through sw-management: `show sw-management software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable]`, for example `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active`, which returns software-load-1-4/active with its sw-component entries, swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label.

Use `show subtype-constraint-<card-type>/<subtype> [min-capacity] [max-capacity] [supported-applications] [unsupported-applications] [description]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `card-type` and `subtype` each represent a group of related PONs for a card type to which the constraints apply, strings of length 1..20. `min-capacity` is the minimum capacity supported by this subtype in gbps and `max-capacity` the maximum in gbps, where -1 means there is no maximum capacity constraint. `supported-applications` and `unsupported-applications` are lists of application type; if either list is empty, that constraint is not applicable. `description` is a string of length 1..255.

Use `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> [state] [version] [description]`, or `show sw-component-<swload-state>/<name> ...` without a location, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The `state` attribute reports the package state: installed (software package installed), not-installed, installation-failed (software package install failed), or unknown, with default unknown, so installation-failed is the value that flags a failed part of the load. `location-id` is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> (0..64), `swload-state` is active, inactive or installable, `name` is the package name (0..256), `version` 0..64 and `description` 0..512. Example: `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`.

Use `show sw-container-<container-name> [equipment] [state] [description] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode; `show sw-container` lists all OS-level containers. `cpu-usage` is the current CPU usage by the container in percentage, range 0...100%, and in a multi-core system it indicates the overall usage relative to all cores. `memory-usage` is current memory usage as a percentage, range 0...100%. `state` is off (default state, not launched yet), up (up and running) or exited. `equipment` is a leafref to the card AID the container runs on, and `uptime` is the time since the container started. Example: `show sw-container-frcu31-1-5_pyapi`.

Yes, with sw-control-rule, which defines service-specific custom rules that override the default action upon service failure. Syntax: `add sw-control-rule-<service-name> fail-action <value>`, plus set, `show sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action]` and `delete sw-control-rule-<service-name>`; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `service-name` is the name of the service to be monitored, String 0..64. `fail-action` values are default-action (performs the policy of restarting the service, then rebooting the system if the service is not recovered), ignore (no automatic action taken on service failure), and system-restart (warm restart of the system/card software immediately upon service failure). Example: `add sw-control-rule-xmm4-1-1_host_KeyManagement fail-action default-action`.

Yes, `show sw-management` shows information about software locations, activity and downloads, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Syntax: `show sw-management [downloads | software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable] | software-load-active | software-load-inactive]`. `downloads` shows download history (the list of downloaded manifest files); `software-load-active` shows active software and `software-load-inactive` shows inactive software, each with its sw-component and packaged-fw entries plus swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label. `software-location-<shelf>-<slot>` narrows the same view to one slot, e.g. `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active`.

Use `show sw-service-<sv-name> [equipment] [location] [state] [state-details] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime] [last-start-time] [reboot-count]`, or `show sw-services` for all services and containers on the node; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `reboot-count` is the number of times a service has restarted, a uint16. `last-start-time` gives the time of the last service start/boot as a date-time YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, and `uptime` is the time since the service turned up in days:hours:minutes. `state` is off (not being monitored), ok (ready and functional) or fail (failed to launch/turn-up or unresponsive), with `state-details` giving a brief description. Example: `show sw-service-frcu31-1-5_host_DpEncrMgr`.

sw-subcomponent goes one level deeper than sw-component: it shows the software load subcomponent details within a named component. Syntax: `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> [state] [version] [description]`, or without location `show sw-subcomponent-<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>`; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. It adds the `sw-component-name` and `sw-subcomponent-name` keys (each string 1..256) to the same attribute set as sw-component: `state` (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown; default unknown), `version` (0..64) and `description` (0..512). Example: `show sw-subcomponent-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg/ztp.deb`.

Run `swversion`. It retrieves the active, inactive and/or installable versions of the software present on the network element, takes no parameters, and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The output lists software-load-active, software-load-inactive and software-load-installable at NE level plus the per-slot equivalents such as software-load-1-1/active, software-load-1-1/inactive and software-load-1-1/installable, each with its version and label, for example `software-load-active R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188`. For the fuller attribute set, use `show software-load-<swload-state>` or `show sw-management`.

Use `show third-party-fw-<fw-name> [file-status] [path] [version] [crc] [vendor] [part-number] [nsa-upgrade-version] [present-in-eqpt] [applicable-eqpt]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `file-status` is the firmware file status with values valid, invalid or missing. `crc` is the cyclic redundancy check of the firmware image, used to validate the file when present (string 0...64). `path` is the path for the firmware image (0...255). `applicable-eqpt` is the list of resources that this firmware can be applied to, and `present-in-eqpt` is the list of resources that contain this version; both have max-elements 80. `nsa-upgrade-version` lists the versions from which the upgrade is non service affecting.

Set it with `set transfer http-proxy <value>`; read it back with `show transfer [debug-log-optional-content] [http-proxy]`. Operational and Candidate configuration mode. `http-proxy` is the proxy server for internally-generated HTTP requests leaving the NE, which includes certificate revocation-related requests, i.e. CRL downloads and OCSP requests. Note that this proxy is not used for file transfers. It is a string of length 0..1024 in the format '[http://]<host>[:<port>]', where 'http://' is optional, '<host>' may be the IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS name of the proxy server, and '<port>' is optional; if <port> is omitted, the default is 1080. Example: `set transfer http-proxy http://1.2.3.4:1080`.

Use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [transfer-type] [session-id] [session-user-name] [filename] [transfer-progress] [bytes-transferred] [total-bytes] [details]`, Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `operation` is upload or download. `transfer-progress` is the transfer completion percentage, 0-100, default 0; `bytes-transferred` and `total-bytes` are uint64 byte counts, both default 0, and total-bytes is zero until known at the transfer start. `details` gives the transfer phase: completed, Failed, idle, preparation or transfer, default idle. `last-completion-status` may be success, fail, in-progress or unknown; unknown occurs if the system reboots while a transfer is in progress. Example: `show transfer-status-trusted-certificate/download`.

Use `show upgrade-status-<resource> [to-swload-version] [status] [start-time] [end-time] [step] [step-start-time] [details]`, Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Status is reported at NE level, chassis level and card level; `resource` (string 0..255) selects the object, and for ne and chassis the results provide aggregated summaries of all cards in that scope, so compare the NE status against per-card ones to locate the failure. `status` values include idle (default), upgrade-in-progress, upgrade-complete, upgrade-partially-failed, upgrade-failed, validate-in-progress/-failed/-complete, apply-in-progress/-failed/-complete, activate-in-progress/-failed/-complete, cancel-in-progress/-complete/-failed and no-communication. `step` names the current upgrade step, with `step-start-time`, `start-time`, `end-time` (each 'na' if idle/unfinished) and `details` (0..255).

Use `upload [-a] [-s] [filetype=]<value> ([destination=]<value> | [file-server=]<value> [[path=]<value>]) ...`, Operational mode, with filetype=debug-log for logs for diagnostic troubleshooting (it includes all other logs). For debug-log the `debug-entity` parameter is mandatory and targets a specific chassis or card; `optional-content` adds optional content. -a uploads asynchronously (check with `show transfer-status`); synchronous mode renders a live progress bar. -s skips TLS verification for HTTPS and ssh known host checking for SCP/SFTP. Certificates differ: for local-certificate and peer-certificate you must specify `certificate-name`; for trusted-certificate omitting the name exports all trusted certificates as a bundle. Only the public part is exported, private keys are not, and output files are in P7 pem format.

Run `show ztp [ztp-mode] [ztp-state] [ztp-details] [ztp-completion-status]`, Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `ztp-state` is the current state of the ZTP service, default ztp-init, with values ztp-init, dhcp-in-progress, image-download-in-progress, image-install-in-progress, custom-script-execution-in-progress, multi-chassis-setup-in-progress, configuration-apply-in-progress, ztp-completed, ztp-state-unknown, ztp-disabled and wait-before-ztp-restart. `ztp-completion-status` summarizes completion on the node as not-completed (default) or completed, and `ztp-details` is a String 0..256 with additional information on the current state. `ztp-mode` is disabled or enabled, default enabled, and is set via the change-ztp-mode RPC, which is allowed even when NBI is locked.

Use the capabilities command: 'show capabilities-<name>', where name is the name of the card (string, no default). It retrieves the information about that card's capabilities. It is a show-only command, available in both Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: 'show capabilities-1-4'. For type-level (rather than instance-level) capability data, the related commands are 'show supported-card-<card-type>', 'show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>', 'show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>' and 'show supported-slot'.

Use the card command. The mandatory parameters on add are required-type, chassis-name and slot-name: 'add card-<name> required-type <value> chassis-name <value> slot-name <value>'. required-type is a String (length 0..32) drawn from the supported card list (BAXOFP2, BLANK, CHM1R, CHM2T, CHM6, CHM7, CHM7X, FAN, FAN-CTRL, FRCU31, ILAx, PEM, RD20TM, SPN2, SPN2C, UCM4, UTM2, XMM4, etc.). chassis-name is String (length 1..255), default 1; slot-name is a String. Optional on add: required-subtype (String 0..32), card-mode (string 0..20), subslot-name (settable only at creation, e.g. 1-2.3), power-profile, alias-name, admin-state (lock/maintenance/unlock, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default Inhibited) and label. Example: 'add card-1-7 chassis-name 1 required-type CHM6 slot-name 7 required-subtype C6 power-profile low'.

On 1830 GX G40, a Native ZR TOM will not come up unless the chassis ambient temperature is configured to 40C. The chassis command documentation states that to bring up a Native ZR TOM the user needs to set the chassis ambient temperature to 40C; if this parameter is not set the system raises a port config mismatch alarm and the TOM cannot be provisioned. Set it with 'set chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature <value>' (number, in Celsius units, no default). configured-ambient-temperature is the configured ambient temperature for the chassis and is used to compute the FRU's power consumption; it is available in add, set and show. Verify with 'show chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature'.

Use the console command: 'set console-<name> [baud-rate <value>] [local-switch <value>]' and 'show console-<name> [baud-rate] [actual-baud-rate] [auto-sensing-state] [local-switch] [status]'. baud-rate values are auto-sensing, 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200. The default is 9600 in 1830 GX G30 and 115200 in 1830 GX G40. Yes, it can work it out itself: in auto-sensing mode the system auto-detects the baud rate from 'ENTER' presses on the serial console client side, then locks it and reports it in actual-baud-rate; auto-sensing-state shows sensing (default) or locked, and is only visible if auto-sensing is enabled. Not all cards support auto-sensing. local-switch is use-global-switch (default), force-enable or force-disable; status shows enabled/disabled.

Use 'show controller-card-<name> [redundancy-status] [redundancy-standby-status] [number-of-switchover-events] [time-of-last-switchover] [additional-details]'. redundancy-status is active, standby or not-in-service (default not-in-service). redundancy-standby-status tells you whether the standby is ready: ready-synchronized (standby is in sync and ready), not-ready-synchronizing (synchronizing data with the active controller, the default), not-ready-synchronize-fail (synchronization failed), lock-out (protection in lock-out state) or card-not-present. additional-details is a string (0..128) with extra synchronization status. number-of-switchover-events (uint32) and time-of-last-switchover are only visible on the active controller card. Example: 'show controller-card-1-12'.

Use the equipment command: 'show equipment [<option>]', available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. With no option it displays all installed equipment; the option is the specific equipment to be viewed, and the available options vary according to the installation. To scope it to one card, name that card, for example 'show equipment card-1-1', which lists the card's child objects (controller-card-1-1, console-1-1, port-1-1-AUX-1, port-1-1-CRAFT, port-1-1-DCN, port-1-1-U1) together with required-type, required-subtype, category, chassis-name, slot-name, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, alias-name, AID, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state, alarm-report-control and label.

Use equipment-policies: 'set equipment-policies [tom-auto-migration <value>] [auto-assigned-directions <value>] [auto-assigned-degrees <value>] [cable-id-control <value>] [chassis-assignment-mode <value>] [comm-eth-location <value>]'. tom-auto-migration (enabled/disabled) enables automatic update of the TOM subtype based on the present equipment; it may directly impact existing configurations, and it covers subtype migration only, not TOM type migration (there is no update between QSFPDD and QSFP28). Degrees are not automatic by default: auto-assigned-degrees (enabled/disabled) defaults to disabled, except enabled when l0-mode-op is hsc-ols. By contrast auto-assigned-directions defaults to enabled. Example: 'set equipment-policies tom-auto-migration enabled'.

SerDes templates are off by default and must be enabled globally with the equipment-templates command: 'set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates <value>' and 'show equipment-templates use-serdes-templates'. Values are enabled/disabled (the CLI value completion offers false and true), and the default is disabled. On enabling, templates are not applied retroactively: they are applied from that moment onward. On disabling there is no impact; the existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs, regardless of whether it was applied via template or manually. Application of serdes-templates depends on this use-serdes-templates flag being true, and re-application can be forced with the 'apply-template' command.

Use the fru-info command: 'show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>'. It displays the packaged FRU information associated with a particular equipment-type. manifest-file is the manifest file, a string of length 0..256; equipment-type is the type of the equipment, a string of length 0..32. The command is show-only and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the data of a physically present FRU (serial number, CLEI, part number, hardware version) use the inventory command instead.

Use the inventory command, which shows the inventory data for a present FRU: 'show inventory-<name> [serial-number] [clei] ...'. Addressing forms are inventory-<name>, inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>, inventory-<card-name>.<slot-name> and inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>. serial-number is the serial number of the equipment (String) and clei is the Common Language Equipment Identifier (String). Other attributes are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision (Number, default 0), PON, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and insertion-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ or 'NA'), number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code (string 0..18, for 3rd party TOMs), actual-power-class (uint8 1..8), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status (not-applicable, current, not-current, unavailable). Example: 'show inventory-1-3-1'.

Use 'show led-<location>/<name> [status]' or 'show leds'. location is the AID of the equipment location of the LED (chassis, card or port AID; string 1..32) and name is the LED name within the FRU (string 1..16). The LED object exists even if the FRU is not physically present, and in that case the status reads not-available. status values are: not-available, off, yellow, flashing-yellow, green, flashing-green, red, flashing-red, cycling-with-off (cycling through all supported colors including off), cycling (cycling through all supported colors excluding off, used for lamp test), amber and flashing-amber. The default is not-available. Example: 'show led status' or 'show leds led-1-1/active'.

In 1830 GX G40 there are three types of ports: comm-eth, USB and trib/line. comm-eth and USB ports are on XMMs only and are found on Slot 1 XMMs. The trib/line ports appear on a CHM6 or CHM7 (slots 4-7) only after a TOM is present/provisioned in the CHM6/CHM7. Port objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. The port-type attribute, shown by 'show port-<card-name>-<port-name> port-type', reports: line (line-side coloured CWDM or DWDM module), tributary (standard grey client interfaces), tributary-subport (a tributary split into subports), usb, comm, uplink (aggregation ports connecting to an adjunct line function), optical, otdr, ocm and pluggable (the port entity represents the L0 module cage for a QSFP/SFP/SFP+ TOM).

Use the resources command: 'show resources-<name> [supported-carriers] [unassigned-carriers] [supported-sub-components] [internal-cell-switch-total-bandwidth] [internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth] [paired-slot-total-bandwidth] [paired-slot-available-bandwidth]'. The bandwidth attributes are applicable only to SPN2/SPN2C cards. internal-cell-switch-total-bandwidth and internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth default to 600.000 Gbit/s if the card has paired slot interconnection capability. paired-slot-total-bandwidth and paired-slot-available-bandwidth apply to SPN2/SPN2C cards that support Paired Slots and default to 500.000 Gbit/s with paired slot interconnection capability, or 0 without it. Example: 'show resources-254-1'.

Read back the status leaf of the serdes object: 'show serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> [value] [status]'. status is the state of the advanced parameter as observable on the system once it is configured, with values: set (parameter set), unknown (parameter unknown, the default), in-progress (parameter in progress), failed (parameter failed) and not-supported (parameter not supported). value is the configured value of the parameter (string). Parameters are created with 'add serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value <value>', edited with set and removed with delete. A plain 'show serdes' lists every serdes entry with its value and status, e.g. serdes-1-7-T1/TxEQ 1 set.

serdes-templates auto-configure serdes for 3rd party TOMs. A template is created per tom-part-number ('add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <value>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>]'); tom-part-number is a string of length 1..16. The template applies to all line cards that support serdes, and when a TOM with that part-number is plugged in the template is applied automatically. Port scope is set with ports-applicable: 'all' (all ports, the default) or a list of port names, each a string of length 1..16, with a maximum of 20 elements (value completion offers T1..T16 and all). Manual serdes configuration is still allowed and is kept even if it deviates from the template. Swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template if one exists. Application depends on use-serdes-templates being true; re-application can be forced with 'apply-template'.

Individual parameters go into a template as serdes-template-entry objects, each composed of a serdes parameter name and its value: 'add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>'. Edit with 'set serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> [value <value>]', remove with delete, and read with 'show serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name>/<name> [value]'. name is the name of the serdes parameter, a string of length 0..256, and value is the value of the serdes parameter, also a string of length 0..256. The template is keyed by tom-part-number (string 1..16). Examples: 'add serdes-template-entry-T-DQ4CNT-NIN/RxEQ value 3' and 'set serdes-template-entry-TR-FC85S-NIN/TxEQ value 2'; typical parameter names are RxAmplitude, RxEQ, RxPreCursor, RxPostCursor, TxEQ and TxEQAdaptive.

Yes. The serial-console object holds the global configuration of all serial console ports in the system: 'set serial-console [global-switch <value>] [global-timeout <value>]' and 'show serial-console [global-switch] [global-timeout]'. global-switch allows access by serial console, with values enabled and disabled, default enabled; each console port can override this global behaviour (the per-card console attribute local-switch takes use-global-switch, force-enable or force-disable). global-timeout is the serial console inactivity timeout, a number in minutes with a default of 60, and it can be set to zero to disable the inactivity timer. The object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: 'set serial-console global-switch enabled global-timeout 80'.

Use the slot command, which shows the slot equipment holder details: 'show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> [AID] [supported-type] [installed-type] [oper-state] [avail-state] [current-equipment]' (or 'show slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>' for a subslot). supported-type is the list of types the holder can take (for example CHM6,gx:UCM4), installed-type is the type currently installed and is empty when no FRU is present, and current-equipment is the name of the equipment currently required in that slot (for example 1-1, shown as --- when none). oper-state is enabled or disabled (default disabled) and avail-state covers values such as normal, in-service, partially-faulted, abnormal, equipment-not-present and equipment-mismatch. 'show slot' lists every slot in the node; 'show slot-1-1' shows just one.

Use the sub-component command, which shows the sub-component details or card resources: 'show sub-component-<card-name>/<sub-component-name> [AID] [description]'. card-name is the name of the card supporting the sub-component (string, length 0..64) and sub-component-name is the name of the sub-component (string). AID is the Resource Access Identifier (string 1..64) and description is a user configurable description (string 0..128). A plain 'show sub-component' lists them all, for example sub-component-1-6/dco-oec with AID 1-6-dco-oec (DCO OEC Optical Engine Controller sub-component) and sub-component-1-6/dco-secproc with AID 1-6-dco-secproc (DCO Security Processor sub-component). The names of sub-components present in a card, which can be addressed for operations such as restart, are also listed by 'show resources-<name> supported-sub-components'.

Use 'show supported-card-<card-type> node-type-compatibility'. node-type-compatibility gives the supported NE node-type for a sled card and is only of relevance for line-card(s) and carrier-card(s). Values are: all (compatible with any node-type), ILA (compatible with the ILA, In-Line Amplifier two-directions, node type) and OADM (Optical Add/Drop Multiplexer node type). So a card is usable on an ILA node if this reads all or ILA. The same command also reports sw-support-revision, supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode, supported-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw in W, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. Example: 'show supported-card-CHM1R'.

Use 'show supported-chassis-<chassis-type> [controller-redundancy-supported] [number-of-front-slots] [number-of-rear-slots] ...'. controller-redundancy-supported is true or false and states whether that chassis type supports controller redundancy. Slot counts come from number-of-front-slots and number-of-rear-slots, both uint8, counting the equipment holder slots in the front and back plates. chassis-type is an identityref such as G31, G32, G34c or G42. The command also shows supported-subtype, default-subtype, description, power-control-supported, fan-adjustment-on-altitude (default false), dust-filter-replacement (not-applicable, optional-dust-filter, dust-filter-regularly-replaced; default optional-dust-filter), depth in mm, height in RUs, leds, supported-subchassis-type (max 10 elements; empty means no multi-chassis support) and supported-features. Example output: supported-chassis-G42, 3RU, redundancy true, 7 front slots, 12 rear slots.

Use 'show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name> [port-type] [direction] [configuration-mode] [faceplate-label] [leds] [present] [default-tom] [parent-port] [subport-list] [allows-auto-migration]'. port-type tells you what the port is for: line, tributary, tributary-subport, usb, comm, uplink, optical, otdr, ocm or pluggable. configuration-mode tells you who provisions it: system-configured (the system configures the card in the slot or TOM in the port and the user cannot make changes) or user-configured (the user can provision or de-provision). Also useful: present (always, or in-node-controller-only), default-tom (default none), faceplate-label (string 1..36), leds (max 10 elements) and allows-auto-migration (true/false, default true), which indicates whether TOMs plugged into this port type are auto migrated per the equipment-policies tom-auto-migration flag. Example: 'show supported-port-CHM1R/2'.

Use 'show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name>' (or supported-slot-<card-type>/<slot-name>). requires-blank-when-empty states whether the slot needs a BLANK filler card when empty, with values not-applicable, optional and required. possible-card-types lists the card types that can go into that slot, with a maximum of 15 elements. The command also reports slot-location (front or rear), slot-vertical-position and slot-horizontal-position (uint8), configuration-mode (system-configured or user-configured), auto-provision-capable (true/false), default-card, reset-power (reset power consumption for the card at 55C, in W), virtual-slot (true/false, default false) and leds (max 10 elements). For example, on a G42 the payload slots 1 and 3..7 are 'required' while FAN and FANCTRL slots are 'not-applicable'.

Use the supported-tom command, which gives the capability information for a supported TOM in the scope of a particular card: 'show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> [supported-subtype] [supported-phy-modes] [default-phy-mode]'. tom-type is the form factor such as CFP2-DCO, QSFP28 or QSFPDD, and tom-subtype-group is a string of length 0..32, for example '4x100GE-breakout'. supported-phy-mode lists the phy-modes supported in that TOM for that card and default-phy-mode is the one used by default; the permitted values for both are 100GE, 200GE, 400GE, 2x100GE, 4x100GE, 100G, 4x10G, 4x10GE, 1GE, 2G5, 10G, 10GE, 2G5E, 40GE, 40G, 4x100G and 200G. Examples: 'show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFP28' and 'show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFPDD/2x100GE-breakout'.

Use 'show supported-tom-power-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type> [supported-power-class] [supported-max-power-draw]'. tom-type is the pluggable form factor (TOM type identity, matching the TOM required-type, for example CFP2-DCO, QSFP28, QSFPDD). supported-power-class is the maximum MSA power class the host port supports for that pluggable type, a uint8 in the range 1..8; the port may only partially support that class, so read it together with supported-max-power-draw, which is the maximum power in watts (decimal64) the host port allows for that pluggable type under supported-power-class. What the pluggable itself reports is on the inventory side: actual-power-class (uint8 1..8) and actual-max-power-draw, populated only for third-party transceiver subtypes on hosts that enforce power-class rules; native qualified subtypes do not populate them.

Yes. When you create a TOM with 'add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>', the Tributary Port termination point is auto-created along with it, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. The add form takes required-type (CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP, SFPPLUS) plus optional required-subtype, phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label, enable-serdes (true/false, default false) and power-mode (powered/not-powered, default powered; only applicable to TOMs on the CHM7 card). Access is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD

Use 'show tom-type-<tom-type> support-third-party-toms'. The support-third-party-toms attribute is a boolean (false, true) that states whether that TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to the supported Nokia TOMs. The same command also shows description (string 0..255), data-rate (uint16, Gbps), and generic-subtype, which is the 3rd party subtype for that TOM. 'show tom-type' with no key lists all supported TOM types. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode and is show-only. When you then fit a third-party module, the tom object has power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), which exists specifically to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

Detected hardware that the Node Controller has not yet accepted in a Multi-Chassis configuration appears under 'show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>'. The AID is keyed by the residing chassis serial number (string 0..16) and the residing slot name (string 0..16); if the equipment is the chassis itself, the slot-name is empty. Attributes you can display are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number (string 1..16), clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, per the set-time command format) and detection-timestamp, which is the last time the Node Controller detected the unprovisioned equipment. Available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use 'show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path]'. usb-path is the local filesystem path where that USB file-system is mounted, a string of length 0..32, and it can be used as the target or source for file transfer operations. available-space is the current free storage and total-space the total storage in the file-system, both uint16 in MB. All three of available-space, total-space and usb-path apply only when type is storage; the other role is power-supply, which powers external equipment such as passive shelves. present (true/false, default false) shows whether the connector is inserted. 'show usb' with no AID lists every USB port on the node. Example: show usb-1-5-U1

Run 'activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]' from Operational mode. The pre-condition is that a snapshot must have been taken before it can be activated, so use take-snapshot first. db-instance names the snapshot to activate and defaults to temp. paraphrase is a short description of the database being activated, a string of length 40...200. sanity-check-override is an action to override the sanity check, values true or false, default false. Examples given are 'activate-snapshot sanity-check-override' and, to activate a snapshot named onehour, 'activate-snapshot onehour'. Existing snapshots can be listed with show database.

Advanced parameter commands can only be executed on the node after 'enable-advanced-parameters' on the optical carrier is set to true. Two documented behaviours explain what you are seeing: if no advanced parameter is configured, or the advanced parameter was deleted, 'show advanced-parameter' reports 'ERROR: object does not exist'; and if an advanced parameter is configured with an invalid value the configuration is not rejected, but 'show advanced-parameter' reports the failed status for it. The status attribute values are failed, in-progress, not-supported, set and unknown, with unknown as the default. The AID form is advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name>, name up to 256 characters. Example: add advanced-parameter-1-4-L1-1/EEPNNLMitigation value "0 1"

Use 'apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*])' from Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. The template-type value serdes-template applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOM list given in the applicable-tom parameter; serdes-templage is listed as the default template-type. applicable-tom is the list of TOMs to apply the serdes-templates against, and if it is not provided (that is, the list is empty) all system TOMs are considered for template application. TOM names are completed for you, for example tom-1-7-T1 through tom-1-7-T15. Example: apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1. Note that the tom object itself carries enable-serdes (false/true, default false), which controls whether configuring TOM SerDes is enabled.

Yes, use a confirmed commit: 'commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>]'. The candidate configuration is committed as usual, but if a confirmation does not occur before the timeout elapses the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version, so the confirmation acts as a persist trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds and defines how long the commit stays pending before rollback; the default rollback time is 10 minutes. To make it permanent run 'commit persist'; to abandon it run 'commit cancel'. For a Persistent Confirmed Commit these commands require the -id parameter, which identifies the commit confirmed, commit persist and confirmed cancel commands. All of these must be run in Candidate Configuration mode, entered with 'configure'. 'commit -m=<message>' attaches a custom message.

Use 'show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)]'. It displays the system configuration, skipping any configuration left at its default value, and the output is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration. Supply an entity-id to narrow the output to one instance, or an entity-type if all entities of that type are relevant. The guide's tip for a replayable form is to run 'show config | display commands' and store the result: that is a good way to create a CLI script that can be used to restore the system configuration. Such a script can then be fed back in, for example via 'configure from-script=<script>' or the initialize-from-script clear-type.

It depends on the target you pick with 'configure <target>'. In exclusive mode only your session can make changes to the candidate configuration; in shared mode multiple sessions can make changes to it. The target values are exclusive and shared, and the default is exclusive. The command runs from Operational mode and moves you into Candidate Configuration mode. You can also control how the candidate datastore is initialized: by default it starts from a copy of the Running Datastore; 'from-default' gives a blank config so you configure from scratch, removing all non-default configuration from the candidate; 'from-script=<script>' imports configuration from a text file of CLI commands; 'from-commit=<commit-id>' initializes from a past commit-record, which is only available when commit-tracking is enabled. Example: configure exclusive

Use 'show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]'. This command shows the current values of the advanced parameters which are actually running on the system, as opposed to 'show advanced-parameter', which reports what you configured plus its status. The AID is keyed by optical-carrier-name and the advanced parameter name, both strings; value is the running value, a string. Run 'show current-advanced-parameter' for everything, or narrow to one carrier, for example 'show current-advanced-parameter-1-4-L2-1/*'. Typical output lists entries such as BOASetting, CRAvgNCtrl, ClockPreEmphasis, EEPNNLMitigation, FastCDAcqTimeCtrl, NLC, PDLMitigation, PMDEquUpdSpeed, RxCDCompCtrl, RxCDMode, RxRollOff, RxVOAMode, TxEqWindowSel, TxHighFreqGain and TxSignalBWControl, and a running value can legitimately differ from the configured one. Access is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

No. 'clear database' performs a full wipe of database contents: it sets the NE database to default and reboots the system, which is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity to the system. It does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data; for a secure wipe or factory default use the 'clear system' command instead. Syntax is 'clear [-f] database [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>', where -f forces the command without confirmation. clear-type is full (reset to factory defaults, the default), keep-networking (wipe but keep network configuration) or initialize-from-script (wipe then initialize from a pre-stored .cli script). keep-networking and initialize-from-script both require new-admin-user and new-admin-password and can only be triggered by the SA user. Expect some transient alarms after the controller card reboot; those can be ignored.

Run 'db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value>' from Operational Mode. The type parameter defines the protection mode to be configured and takes either encryption-with-integrity or encryption. To get integrity protection in addition to encryption, use encryption-with-integrity; that command enables the integrity check for the system database and automatically reboots the controller. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Example: db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity. Afterwards confirm the result with 'show db-protection-scheme', where mode reads encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and is documented as changeable via the db-migrate RPC, integrity-algorithm reads hmac-sha2-512 or none, and integrity-status reads passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled.

Run 'show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode]'. The integrity-status attribute indicates the status of the integrity check and reads passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled; disabled means integrity is not in use. integrity-algorithm is the integrity algorithm used for the DB, either hmac-sha2-512 or none. mode is the current protection scheme, either encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, and can be changed via the db-migrate RPC. encryption-algorithm is xts-aes-256-plain64, AES-256 encryption in XTS mode with 64-byte block size. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. A node that has not been migrated shows integrity-algorithm none, integrity-status disabled and mode encryption-only.

Use 'diff [-t|-c] candidate', which compares the candidate configuration with the current system configuration and must be run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It lists created, deleted and changed objects and displays only configurable attributes; in the diff, new data is the candidate configuration and old data is the current system configuration. Output forms are: normal diff style, where + marks added objects or new values and - marks deleted objects or old values; side-by-side table style with the -t flag; and yes, as CLI commands that would reproduce the candidate changes with the -c flag. The -d flag gives a CLI command listing of the commands being executed.
