'diff commit <id> [<id>]' compares a commit-record against the running configuration or another commit-record, cumulatively, and is only available when commit-records exist (commit-tracking enabled) or a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Run 'discard-changes'. It discards all candidate datastore content and returns the CLI to operational mode. The command takes no parameters and is only accepted in Candidate Configuration mode. If instead of throwing everything away you want to step back to an earlier committed state, use 'rollback commit [<commit-id>]', which on the candidate datastore is only possible when the candidate is empty.

An extended-config is a non-standard configuration that introduces exceptional behavior globally in the system, so treat it with care. Commands are 'add extended-config-<name>', 'delete extended-config-<name>' and 'show extended-config-<name> [description]', available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Using it requires knowledge of the extended-config name on the user side, and the name must match a name already known by the system; name is a string of length 0..64. The description attribute (string 0..255) is supplied by the system and states what that extended-config is and its effect in the system, so read it with 'show extended-config-<name> description' before adding one.

Check the Golden Advanced Parameter Table with 'show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> [description] [type] [supported-values] [direction] [multiplicity] [configuration-impact] [service-impact]'. The service-impact attribute states whether applying that parameter change causes service impact: values are service-affecting or non-service-affecting. If it is service-affecting, you must perform an admin lock or maintenance operation, or other relevant operations, before applying it. configuration-impact tells you what configuration steps apply the change: no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change or full-config-no-pll-change. Also useful are supported-values (list of ranges or discrete numbers), direction (transmit, receive, transmit-and-receive) and multiplicity (uint8, how many values you must enter). All attributes are read-only. Example: show golden-advanced-parameter-chm7/EEPNNLMitigation

Use 'lock' from Operational Mode. It locks database access to the current session, granting your CLI session exclusive write access, and is intended for ensuring configuration mastership for a small time. While the database is locked, any other session, CLI or otherwise, that tries to make a configuration change receives an error, and a lock is not possible if another session already holds it. The lock is released either by the 'unlock' command or by closing the session that took the lock, explicitly by the user, by an administrator closing the session, or by inactivity time-out. Only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock; unlocking a database that is not locked, or that was locked by another session, fails. After unlock any session can configure again or take a new lock. Both commands accept only the -h help flag.

A named-value-set is addressed by a two-part key: named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>, where db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user-assigned name for that named-value-set. It holds a single value attribute, a string of length 1..1024 characters. The commands are 'add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>]', 'set ... [value <value>]', 'show ... [value]' and 'delete ...', all available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. db-entry-name and named-value-set-name are used in add, set, show and delete.

Only if recovery from chassis storage is configured for it. Use 'set recovery restore-from-chassis-storage <value>' and 'show recovery [restore-from-chassis-storage] [restore-status] [backup-status] [last-backup] [next-backup]'. The values are disabled (chassis storage is not used for restoration on this NE), auto-restore (SW and DB are stored on chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, then a manual 'clear recovery-mode' is needed, which lets you validate the restored system before affecting the hardware), and auto-in-service (SW and DB are restored in recovery mode and on successful restore the Node Controller automatically leaves recovery mode). The default is auto-in-service. restore-status reads init, image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade or wait-for-db-restore; backup-status reads successful, failed, in-progress or unknown; last-backup and next-backup are timestamps or never.

Only if the candidate is empty. 'rollback commit [<commit-id>]' must be executed with the commit parameter and optionally a specific commit-id; if no commit-id is given the most recent commit-record is used. It works in the Running Datastore (the default) or in the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if that candidate is empty, which is one way to initialize the candidate. The command considers all commit records up to the provided commit-id, obtains the reverse-commands for each record, and replays them in order from latest to oldest, reverting the datastore to the state it was in prior to that commit-record. Access is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. Since it relies on commit-records, the commit-tracking system-policy has to be enabled for records to exist. If you simply want to drop staged changes, use discard-changes.

'show commit [<id>|-s=<since>|-n=<number-of-records>]' retrieves commit record information and lets you visualize the Commit Repository, but it is available only when the commit-tracking policy is enabled, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists. If neither is true on your node there are no commit-records to show. Enable the repository with 'set system-policies commit-tracking enabled'; the commit-tracking default is disabled, and disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. Check the current state with 'show system-policies commit-tracking'. The flags are -n to select an exact number of records, -s to pick a timestamp and show all records created since it, and <id> to select a specific commit-record. Access is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'set system-policies [commit-tracking <value>] [writable-running <value>]' and 'show system-policies [commit-tracking] [writable-running]', available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. commit-tracking enables the commit-repository feature: with it enabled, all configuration changes made via the running or candidate datastores are stored as commit-records, which can then be visualized, compared and rolled back. Its values are enabled and disabled, default disabled, and disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. The running datastore is writable by default: writable-running is also enabled/disabled with default disabled, and disabling writable-running makes it impossible to issue configure commands via the running datastore, forcing use of the candidate. In that state the CLI allows add/set/delete only in Candidate mode, NETCONF allows edit-config only via the candidate, and RESTCONF, gNMI (telemetry still allowed, gNOI still allowed), WebGUI and TL1 become read-only.

The db-passphrase. The system only accepts take-snapshot if the db-passphrase used for DB snapshot encryption is configured, either globally as part of the security-policies ('set security-policies db-passphrase') or locally as a parameter of the command ('take-snapshot db-passphrase=***'). The passphrase must be a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain any dictionary words, and may use special characters in accordance with the 85-character Z85 set. Automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. Syntax is 'take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]' in Operational Mode. db-instance is temp (default, temporary storage for manual backup and restore), manual (permanent storage), or the automatic onehour, oneday, oneweek, plus rollback; description is a string 0...128. Taking a snapshot that already exists overwrites the existing file. List snapshots with show database.

Use the `template` command. A template is a single entry defined by an object/attribute pair plus the value to use as that attribute's default: `add template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> object <value> attribute <value> value <value> [sequence-id <value>] [label <value>] [condition <value>]`. `object` is the object name (for example odu), `attribute` the attribute name (for example admin-state), and `value` the value to apply (for example lock) and is mandatory. `sequence-id` is a number in range 1..65535 that sets the processing order, lower ids first. `condition` is optional and restricts application (for example service-type=OTU4); `label` is optional. Use `set` to change fields, `show` to display them and `delete template-<group>/<name>` to remove the entry. Example: `add template-1/FansInMaintenance object card attribute admin-state value maintenance condition card-type=FAN`. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. A template-group is created with `add template-group-<name> [enabled <value>] [label <value>]`, where `enabled` takes true or false. Its default is true only if there is no other template-group enabled, so a second group cannot come up enabled while one is already active. The template-group is the configuration group holding the list of template entries; `name` and `label` are strings. Use `show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label]` to check state and `delete template-group-<name>` to remove one. Example: `add template-group-1` creates and enables the group. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show templates`. It displays the configuration that defines the data model for system templates, giving the overall view of templates on the node. It takes no parameters and is available in both Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the individual layers below it, use `show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label]` for a group and `show template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> [sequence-id] [object] [attribute] [value] [label] [condition]` for a single template entry.

No. `unlock` releases a database previously locked with the `lock` command, but only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock. If a session tries to unlock a non-locked database, or one locked by another session, the `unlock` command fails. The lock is released automatically if the session that took it is closed, so the lock will clear when the other operator's session ends. After a successful unlock, any session can configure again and take a new lock. Syntax is `unlock [-h]`, where `-h` displays help; access mode is Operational Mode.

Yes, use `validate candidate <candidate> command <string>`. It validates the contents of the specified configuration, checking any CLI command used to edit a configuration datastore by creating, deleting, merging or replacing content, without applying it. `candidate` is the candidate datastore targeted for validation and `command` is the command string to validate; both are strings with no default. If the command validates, the reply is 'OK'; otherwise the command fails. Multiple CLI commands can be supplied in one call if separated with ';'. Example: `validate 'set ne altitude 600'`. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `add additional-key-exchange-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<additional-key-exchange-id> dh-group <value>`. A maximum of 7 rounds can be configured (additional-key-exchange-id 1..7) and each round must use a unique key-exchange algorithm. The rounds must be configured in the same order on both IKE peers; if the configuration does not match, an IKE-CONFIG-MISMATCH alarm is raised. Configuring additional-key-exchange is optional, and doing so brings the IKE session down immediately so it renegotiates the new proposal. Child SA (port level) key exchange is derived from IKE. `dh-group` values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512, ml-kem-768, ml-kem-1024. For PQC safety, configure PPK or at least one post-quantum algorithm; ml-kem-1024 is recommended as the strongest.

Use `show data-path-encryption`. This command shows the datapath encryption attributes. It takes no parameters, and its access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The related global policy is set with the `ikev2` command: `set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <match|ignore>`, an L1 encryption-specific policy for whether the NE validates the certificate subject alternate name against the IKE ID.

Use the `encryption-algorithm` command, where the algorithm and key length are part of the AID: `add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>` (a variant without the SPD entry name applies to the IKE SA). Permitted `algorithm` values are null, aes-gcm-8, aes-gcm-12, aes-gcm-16, aes-ctr, aes-cbc, aes-ccm-8, aes-ccm-12, aes-ccm-16 and chacha20-poly1305. Permitted `key-length` values are none, key-length-128, key-length-192 and key-length-256, with a default of none. `number` is the proposal number for the IKE SA, range 1..max. Only add, show and delete are supported. Example: `add encryption-algorithm-ipsec/GX2/1/aes-gcm-8/key-length-192`.

With `add ike-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number> integrity-algorithm <value> dh-group <value> [prf <value>]`, both `integrity-algorithm` and `dh-group` are mandatory; `prf` is optional. `integrity-algorithm` values: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. `dh-group` values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512. `prf` values: hmac-sha2-256, hmac-sha2-384, hmac-sha2-512, hmac-sha1. `number` is the proposal number, range 1..max. `protocol-id` is read-only and always IKE. Example: `add ike-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/1 dh-group dhe-2048 prf hmac-sha2-256 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-384-192`.

The top-level `ikev2` object carries a single attribute, `data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match`. It is a global, L1 encryption-specific policy indicating whether the NE must validate the certificate subject alternate name to match the IKE ID (OPT-IN) or not (OPT-OUT). Permitted values are `match` and `ignore`, with no default stated. Syntax: `set ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <value>]` and `show ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match]`. Example: `set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match match`. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show ikev2-local-instance-<name> host-card-encryption-capability`: it indicates whether the card on which this IKEv2 local instance runs supports encryption, with values yes, no or unknown and a default of unknown. It is read-only (show). The address is governed by `local-address-assignment-method`, a read-only attribute with values auto or manual, default auto. `local-address` is the local IPv4 address for the IKEv2 channel with prefix-length 32, default 0.0.0.0, and is settable: `set ikev2-local-instance-1-3 local-address 1.1.180.132`. Other settable attributes are `scope` (data-path-encryption, management-ipsec, local-address, local-address-assignment-method), `label`, `admin-state` (lock, maintenance, unlock; default unlock) and `alarm-report-control` (allowed, inhibited; default Inhibited). `host-card`, `started-time`, `AID` and `oper-state` (enabled/disabled, default disabled) are show only.

On `ikev2-peer`, `re-key-frequency` is the IKE SA re-key frequency, range 3600..86400 seconds with default 28800; `re-auth-frequency` is the re-authentication frequency, range 3600..604800 seconds with default 43200. The stated rule: re-key-frequency and re-auth-frequency must not be multiples of each other, and they must differ by a few minutes so there is a significant interval between re-authentication and re-keying. Related attributes are `re-key-fail-policy` (kill traffic, continue traffic; default continue-traffic) with `re-key-traffic-kill-offset` (0..86400 seconds, default 0), and `re-auth-fail-policy` with `re-auth-traffic-kill-offset` (0..86400 seconds, default 0), which set how long the system waits before killing the encrypted SAs or Child SAs tied to the IKE SA.

Use `add ipsec-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number> dh-group <value> [integrity-algorithm <value>]`. `dh-group` is mandatory and `integrity-algorithm` optional. `dh-group` values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448. `integrity-algorithm` values: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. `number` is the proposal number, range 1..max, and `ipsec-spd-entry-name` is a string of length 1..32. Two read-only attributes appear in show: `protocol-id`, values ESP with default ESP, and `esn` (Extended Sequence Number support), value esn with default esn. Example: `add ipsec-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/dns/1 dh-group dhe-3072 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512-256`.

Yes. `ipsec-sa-re-key-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>` supports three re-key triggers for the IPsec child SA with the far-end peer. `frequency` is time-based, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 14400. `bytes` re-keys on the amount of bytes transmitted, range 1048576..max, default 1073741824. `packets` re-keys on the amount of packets transmitted, values disabled or a number in the range 1..9223372036854775808, default disabled. All three are available with add, set and show; use `delete ipsec-sa-re-key-<...>` to remove the object. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

The `action` attribute of `ipsec-spd-entry` indicates the IPsec treatment given to matching IP datagrams. Values are protect, bypass and discard, with a default of protect. Tunnelling is controlled separately by `mode`, values tunnel or transport, default tunnel, so yes, the entry tunnels by default. `priority` (number, uint8) is mandatory on add and gives precedence between SPD entries. `ipsec-protocol` is ESP (default ESP). `esn` is true or false, default true. `anti-replay-window` applies when action = protect, range 32..1024, default 64. `alarm-report-control` is allowed or inhibited, default allowed, and `dynamic-ts` is disabled or enabled, default disabled. Example: `add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect`.

Create a traffic selector under the SPD entry: `add ipsec-traffic-selector-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name> [next-layer-protocol <value>]`. `next-layer-protocol` indicates the inner (upper layer) protocol obtained from the IPv4 protocol or IPv6 next header field; values are any (value 0), opaque (value 255) or a number in the range 0-255, default any. The selector name is a string of length 1..64 with pattern '([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*)'. The addresses and ports themselves are then attached beneath the selector using the `local-subnet`, `remote-subnet`, `local-ports` and `remote-ports` commands. Example: `add ipsec-traffic-selector-ipsec/GX2/Radius/ts1 next-layer-protocol 17`.

Because the port range is part of the object's key, not an editable attribute. The `local-ports` command only supports add, show and delete, and the AID itself carries the range: `add|show|delete local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>`. `start` accepts all, opaque or a port number; `stop` is a port-number and defaults to 0, but 0 is only accepted by the system if the starting port is set to all or opaque. To change a range, delete the existing entry and add the new one. Examples: `add local-ports-ipsec/GX2/tacacs/ts1/all` and, for a single port with start=stop=53, `add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53`.

Use `add local-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>`. The `prefix` is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, or broadcast for IPv4 only) and is part of the AID, so only add, show and delete are supported; there is no set. Example: `add local-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/101.10.10.1/32`. Use `show local-subnet-<...>/<prefix>` to display it and `delete local-subnet-<...>/<prefix>` to remove it. The traffic selector must already exist under the SPD entry. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

That depends on `link-security-control` on the `macsec-entity`, which controls the link security policy for handling data packets when the MACsec connection is not available. Values are must-secure and should-secure, with a default of must-secure, so by default traffic is not passed unsecured. Set it with `set macsec-entity-<name> link-security-control <value>`. Other attributes: `enabled` (true, false; default true), `supporting-facility` (the supporting facility name), `alarm-report-control` (allowed, inhibited; default Inhibited), `replay-protection` (enable, disable) and `replay-protection-window` (range 0..4294967295, default 0). `negotiated-cipher-suite`, `AID` and `oper-state` are show only. Example: `add macsec-entity-6-3-3 supporting-facility ethernet-6-3-3`.

Use the `macsec-mka` command: `set macsec-mka-<name> connectivity-association-key <value> connectivity-association-key-name <value>`. Both the pre-shared Connectivity Association Key and its name are strings of length 0..64. To see which end is key server, read the `is-key-server` attribute with `show macsec-mka-<name>`; values are true or false, default false. Other attributes are `mka-policy` (the mka policy name to use), `label`, `alarm-report-control` (allowed, inhibited; default Inhibited), `psk-lifetime`/`psk-expiration-warning` (range 1..173, default 14 days), `psk-lifetime-enable` (enabled, disabled) and the read-only `psk-configured-timestamp` and `AID`. Example: `set macsec-mka-6-3-3 connectivity-association-key 1122334411223344556677889900112233445566778899001122334455667788 connectivity-association-key-name aa`.

Both live on `mka-policy`, the MACsec Key Agreement policy referenced by the macsec entity related to the ethernet facility: `add|set mka-policy-<name> [key-server-priority <value>] [macsec-cipher-suite <value>] [confidentiality-offset <value>] [sak-rekey-interval <value>]`. `macsec-cipher-suite` selects the cipher suites for Secure Association Key (SAK) derivation. `sak-rekey-interval` is the SAK rekey interval in seconds, range '0|30..65535', default 30s. `key-server-priority` is the priority used by the MKA protocol to select the key server. `confidentiality-offset` specifies a number of octets in an Ethernet frame sent in unencrypted plain text. Use `show mka-policy-<name>` to display them and `delete mka-policy-<name>` to remove the policy. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the `re-auth` command, which performs a re-authentication operation of IKEv2 security associations. Syntax: `re-auth [ikev2-peer=]<value>`, where `ikev2-peer` is a string reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA). Access mode is Operational mode only. Examples: `re-auth ikev2-peer=ikev2-NE202` and `re-auth ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX2`. Note this is separate from the scheduled `re-auth-frequency` on the ikev2-peer object; re-auth triggers the operation immediately.

The `re-key` command performs an on-demand re-key on one of three targets: a data path encryption secure entity, an IKEv2 peer, or an IPsec child security association (Security Policy Database entry). Syntax: `re-key [ipsec-security-association=]<value> | [ikev2-peer=]<value> | [secure-entity=]<value>`. `ipsec-security-association` points to the IPsec SPD entry object (Child SA), `ikev2-peer` is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), and `secure-entity` points to the secure entity object (Child SA); all are strings. Access mode is Operational mode. Examples: `re-key secure-entity=NE202-1-4-L1-1` and `re-key ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX`.

Set the starting port to `all` and omit the stopping port: `add remote-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/all`. The `start` parameter accepts all, opaque or a port number. `stop` is a port-number; if the stopping port is not set, the system assumes 0, and the value 0 is only accepted when the starting port is set to all or opaque. Only add, show and delete are supported because the range is part of the AID. Examples: `add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all` for every port and `add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/49/49` for a single port.

Use `add remote-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>`. The `prefix` is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, or broadcast for IPv4 only) and forms part of the AID, so only add, show and delete are available; there is no set. Example: `add remote-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/102.20.20.2/32`. Display with `show remote-subnet-<...>/<prefix>` and remove with `delete remote-subnet-<...>/<prefix>`. The ikev2 local instance, peer, SPD entry and traffic selector named in the AID must already exist. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the sc-rx (Receiving Secure Channel) show command: show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. The state attribute is the one that tells you whether the channel is being used: it is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack, with values in-use (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use) and not-in-use (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). The AID is composed of name, a string of length 0..64, and index, the Receiving Secure Channel Index (uint8). sci-rx is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

sc-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel object and it is show-only; there is no add, set or delete form. Syntax: show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. name is a string of length 0..64 and index is the Transmitting Secure Channel Index (uint8). sci-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. state is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack, either in-use (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel is in use) or not-in-use (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). It also reports association-number, key-identifier and next-packet-number. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application represents an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. The certificate it presents is chosen with set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <value>, a string of length 0..128 that is a list of assigned certificates; multiple certificates are comma separated, for example set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY. show secure-application-<id> reports type (server or client), active-certificate-id, in-use (leafref to ../active-certificate-id, i.e. the certificate actually active), status (enabled or disabled) and verify-client-cert. To demand a client certificate, set verify-client-cert required; this enables TLS Mutual Authentication and the client certificate is required and validated. The default is disabled, meaning no client certificate is requested. Changes only affect new TLS connections, not existing ones. show secure-applications lists them all.

That is governed by re-key-fail-policy on the secure-entity. It indicates the NE policy and consequent action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful, and takes kill-traffic or continue-traffic, with continue-traffic as the default, so by default traffic is not dropped. If you set kill-traffic, traffic-kill-offset defines how long the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to that IKE SA; its range is 0..86400 seconds with a default of 0. The related re-key-frequency is the re-key frequency for the IKE security association with the far-end IKE peer, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800. All three are settable on add secure-entity-<name> and set secure-entity-<name>, for example: add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity '1-4-L1-1' re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is a show-only object: show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group]. Every attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: number is 1, encryption-algorithm is aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length is key-length-256, integrity-algorithm is none, and dh-group is ecp-521 (the Diffie-Hellman group advertised to the far-end secure entity peer). There is no add or set form, so the algorithm suite is fixed by the system and can only be inspected. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Through the security-policy-database object, whose key is the pair <ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>: add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>]. ikev2-local-instance is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance and ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA); both are strings. associated-secure-entity is the list of all SPD entries associated with that far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). set, show and delete use the same key. Example on the 1830 GX G40: add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with a CRL Distribution Point. Each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL: add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>]. url is the HTTP URL of the CRL in the form 'http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>', where host may be an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the file conventionally uses the .crl extension, for example http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. enabled (true/false, default false) enables automatic download and periodic refresh; enabling immediately triggers a CRL auto-download, and while disabled no refresh or updates occur but existing CRLs are unaffected. refresh-interval accepts the special enum use-next-update (next refresh taken from the current CRL next-update field) or a duration written as '[xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs]', for example 2w, or 5d 12h. show cdp-<name> reports next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result; show cdps lists all. Requires System Administrator privilege.

Use cert-gen in Operational mode: cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]. certificate-name is a string of length 1..128. days is the number of days the certificate is valid for and defaults to 365. org-name and common-name are strings of length 1..64; subject is the full certificate subject name, string length 1..1024. When generating a self-signed certificate you must specify either subject or common-name. auto-install (true/false, default true) auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application that has no active certificate. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Example: cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true.

With cert-to-name, a prioritized set of rules that map an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity: add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>]. map-type is either extract (take the identity from a certificate field) or map (use an explicit username). field applies only when map-type is extract and selects the certificate attribute used: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn or san-uri. mapped-user-name is required only when map-type is map and names the local or remote user. criteria defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked. priority ranges 1 to 255. issuer adds a restriction filtering certificates from a specific issuer (value any). enabled defaults to True. Example: add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name.

Use clear certificate, in Operational mode: clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>. type is trusted, local or peer, and id is the certificate ID (string length 0..128); the id must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type, and <tab> gives the list of certificate-ids that can be cleared. -f forces the command; otherwise you are prompted 'Are you sure? [y/n]'. Examples: clear certificate local certX, clear certificate type=trusted id=certY. type also accepts bulk purge options: purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. To list what is installed, run show certificates, which displays all managed local/trusted/peer X509v3 certificates imported by download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; show certificate-revocation shows certificate revocations.

Use clear crl with a clear-target: clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value>. The targets are single-crl (the default, removes only the CRL named in <crl-name>, which is mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL), purge-invalid-crls (purge all invalid CRLs), purge-cached-crls (purge all CRLs automatically cached from a configured CDP or a certificate CDP extension) and purge-all-crls (purge all CRLs). To drop only stale entries use clear crl purge-invalid-crls; to drop just the auto-downloaded copies use purge-cached-crls. Use <tab> to list CRL names that can be cleared, and omit <crl-name> for the purge targets. Check first with show crls or show crl-<name>, whose status attribute reads valid, expired or future and whose type attribute reads cached or manually. The clear form is Operational mode only; show also works in Candidate Configuration mode.

csr-gen creates a local-certificate in the 'pending-import' state and outputs a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is then signed by an external Certificate Authority and the resulting full certificate is downloaded into the system to complete the local-certificate. Until then, show local-certificate-<id> reports status pending-import (the status list documents 'If CSR pending - pending-import'). Syntax: csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [subject=] [SAN=] [key-usage=] [extended-key-usage=]. key-algorithm defaults to eccp256; signature-hash-algorithm defaults to sha256 for rsa2048/rsa3072/eccp256, sha384 for eccp384 and sha512 for rsa4096/eccp521. The subject must include the CN RDN. Operational mode only.

Use display-cert with the display-type parameter: display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>. display-type takes all-certificate-hierarchy, certificate-details or certificate-hierarchy, and defaults to all-certificate-hierarchy, so a bare display-cert already gives you the hierarchy rather than only the certificate body; use display-type=certificate-details when you want just that certificate's own details. The certificate parameter is the certificate to display, and tab completion offers the installed names such as local-certificate-pace_client, local-certificate-server_cert, trusted-certificate-ca_root and trusted-certificate-pace_root, for example display-cert trusted-certificate-ca_root. The command also shows CSRs. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The trust chain of a specific certificate is also visible as the trust-chain attribute of show local-certificate-<id> or show peer-certificate-<id>.

Use the est command, which drives the Enrollment over Secure Transport client and replaces the manual CSR workflow: est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [subject=] [SAN=] [key-usage=] [extended-key-usage=] [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]. target-command selects cacerts, enroll or re-enroll. est-ca names the CA set for EST and defaults to 1. key-algorithm accepts eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072 or rsa4096; signature-hash-algorithm is sha512, sha384 or sha256, default sha256; metadata-template is from-existing-certificate, from-openssl-cnf, generic, generic-tls-server, generic-tls-client or generic-ikev2-identity, default generic. Use http-user/http-password when no valid mTLS certificate exists: est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>.

Yes, via set est-ca-<name> auto-re-enrollment <value>. It specifies how far before expiration re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by that EST CA. Accepted values are a number of days before expiration from 1 to 365, or a percentage of the elapsed certificate lifetime ('not after date' minus 'not before date', rounded up) from 10% to 90% in 10% increments, or disabled. The default is Disabled, so automatic re-enrollment is off until you configure it. Example: set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40. If auto re-enrollment fails for any reason, the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until it succeeds or the certificate becomes invalid, for example through expiration. The CA is pinned with explicit-ca-root, the trusted root certificate for the EST CA, and root-fingerprint, which verifies the identity of the Root CA using a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash to ensure a secure initial connection.

The EST server port is set with server-port on the est-server object and defaults to 443. Syntax: add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>], with matching set, delete and show forms. Yes, you can define more than one: each entry is keyed by <name>/<server-name>, and priority defines the server's precedence with a value range of 1 to 10. If priority is omitted it defaults to the current lowest precedence (highest existing number) plus one; if a priority of 10 already exists, the value must be configured manually. enabled is True or False, default True. path-segment is an optional label added to the EST base url, a string of length 0..64. Example: add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format directly into the NE: import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]. The certificate type is local-certificate, trusted-certificate or peer-certificate. certificate-name is the name the certificate will be known by in the system. The PEM string carries the certificate(s) and, where applicable, private keys; passphrase decodes encrypted input and applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. The -i flag imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM bundle in addition to the leaf certificate, and for a single-certificate file it imports intermediates specified through the AIA extension; root certificates must be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, for example trusted-certificate-Nokia-1. -h shows help. Operational mode.

Check the ISK object before clearing it: show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time], or show ISKs for the list. is-key-in-use indicates whether the key is in use in this FRU (true/false, default false) and is-key-verified indicates whether the key is verified in this FRU (true/false, default false). being-deleted is set to true once the system receives an ISK delete command, meaning deletion is already in progress. KRK-name names the Image Root Key that signed this ISK. To remove one, use clear [-f] isk [key-name=]<value>, supplying the name of the key to be deleted, for example clear isk key-name=name; -f forces the command without confirmation. show works in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode; clear is Operational mode.

Use the KRK commands, which show the list of Image Root Keys and per-key information: show KRKs lists them all, and show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] shows one, for example show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1. The attributes are name (unique representation of the object), CPU (identifier for member CPUs on cards, starting at 0, uint8), key-name (string length 0..64), key-serial-number (string), issuer-name (name of the CSA, Code Signing Appliance, string length 0..20), key-length (key length in bits, uint16) and key-payload (key payload in hex format, string length 0..1100). KRK is show-only, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The KRK that signed a given Image Signing Key is reported as the KRK-name attribute of show ISK.

Use show key-replacement-package, which displays the key replacement package (KRP) attributes: show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]. KRP-version is the package version, issuer-name is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance, string length 0..20), and KRK-name is the name of the KRK (Image root key) that signed this ISK. signature-hash-scheme is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512; signature-algorithm is ECDSA, RSA or none; signature-payload is a hex string of 0..1024; signature-gen-time is a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. install-status indicates whether this KRP has been installed in the system and reads not-installed, installing, installed or failed. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Each local-certificate has a revocation-mode attribute that controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined, with values auto, force-revoked and force-unrevoked and a default of auto. Setting force-revoked makes the node treat the certificate as revoked regardless of CRL or OCSP results, and force-unrevoked forces the opposite. Syntax: set local-certificate-<id> [revocation-mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]. The id is a string of length 1..128. show local-certificate-<id> reports revocation-mode along with status (pending-import, expired, revoked, untrusted, future or valid), trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, self-signed and used-by, the list of secure-applications, ikev2-peers and so on presently using the certificate. The same revocation-mode attribute with the same auto/force-revoked/force-unrevoked values and auto default exists on peer-certificate. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>]. url is the HTTP URL of the OCSP responder in the form 'http://<host>[:<port>]' where host may be an IPv4/v6 address or a DNS name and the port is optional, otherwise the default HTTP port 80 is used; it is a string of length 0..1024 matching the pattern 'http://([^\s/$.?#][^\s/]*)'. priority sorts the OCSP responders in order of precedence, a uint8 in the range 1..10, and lower numbered responders are consulted before higher numbered ones, so priority 1 is tried first. enabled (true/false, default false) controls whether this server is consulted for revocation status. name is a string of length 0..64. show ocsp-server-<name> also reports last-query, the timestamp of the last successful query (never or a date-and-time). Example: add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true. set changes priority and enabled; delete removes the entry.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate that represents a trusted 'remote peer' certificate for the L1 encryption secure application. The white-listed attribute (true/false, default false) means that when true the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; when false it has an associated trust-chain, listed in trust-chain as a leafref to /ne/system/security/certificates/trusted-certificate/id. white-listed is read-only in show peer-certificate[-id], alongside version, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, valid-from, valid-to, status, public-key-length, public-key-type, signature-key-type, signature-hash-algorithm, certificate-bytes and subject-alternative-names. The settable attributes are alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label (string 0..256) and revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked, default auto).

The ssh object gives direct access to shell via ssh, and it is off by default: enabled is true/false with a default of false. The listening port is set with the port attribute, a number in the range 1..65535 with a default of 8022, described as the port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell. Syntax: set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>] and show ssh [enabled] [port] [pre-login-message] [post-login-message]. pre-login-message is the welcome message displayed before user login (string 0..1440, no default) and post-login-message is displayed after login and has a default warning banner stating the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes and may be monitored. The object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add an ssh-authorized-key entry for that user; each entry holds a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Syntax: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>], with set (label only), show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label] and delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>. user-name is the user owning the authorized key and can be a local or remote user (string 0..32); key-id is a unique identifier for the entry (string 1..64). public-key is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) public key component encoded in PEM format as '<key type><SPACE>...base64 encoded OpenSSH public key...<SPACE><comment>', a string of 0..2048 characters. The read-only public-key-algorithm reports ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. Example: add ssh-authorized-key-admin/1 public-key AAAAE2VjZHNhLXNoYTItbmlzdHA1MjEA...

The node's global SSHv2 host keys (used by both server-side and client-side SSHv2 apps) are shown with 'show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm> [public-key] [label] [fingerprint-algorithm] [fingerprint]'. There must be one host key per supported algorithm, so yes, more than one exists. The system auto-generates a host-key in the default DB, and additional host-keys can be added or overwritten via the ssh-keygen RPC. Supported public-key-algorithm values: ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096, ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 support starts in R9.0). public-key is PEM-encoded OpenSSH format, string 0..2048 characters; label is a string 0..256; fingerprint-algorithm is md5 or sha256; fingerprint is a string 0..95 characters of hex digit pairs. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration. Example: show ssh-host-key-ecdsa-sha2-nistp521.

ssh-keygen generates an SSH private/public key pair and the existing keys in the system are replaced with the newly generated pair. Syntax: ssh-keygen [-b=<Key-length>] [-l=<key-label>] [-t=<type>], available in Operational mode only. -t selects rsa, ecdsa or ed25519, defaulting to rsa. -b sets strength: RSA 2048, 3072 or 4096 (default 2048), ECDSA 256, 384 or 521 (default 256), ED25519 256. If secure mode is enabled (see security-policies/secure-mode), RSA only supports 4096 and ECDSA supports 384 or 521 (default 384); ED25519 stays at 256 regardless of secure mode. -l sets the key label; with no value the label becomes the ne-id value. The resulting public key is retrieved with 'show ssh-host-key'.

Pre-trust an outbound SSH peer by adding an SSHv2 known-hosts entry: 'add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label <value>]'. Also available: set ssh-known-host-<id> [label] (only the label is settable afterwards), show ssh-known-host-<id> [address] [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label], and delete ssh-known-host-<id>. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration. id is a unique name, string 0..64 characters. address is the hostname, IPv4 or IPv6 address of the allowed/known peer host, optionally with a %zone-index. public-key-algorithm is ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096 or ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 from R9.0). public-key is the PEM/OpenSSH-format public key component, string 0..2048 characters; label is 0..256 characters.

The trusted-certificate object holds the X509v3 CA (Root and Intermediate) certificates trusted by the system. Commands: 'set trusted-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>]' and 'show trusted-certificate[-id]' with attributes version, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, status, public-key-length, public-key-type, signature-key-type, signature-hash-algorithm, certificate-bytes, key-usage, extended-key-usage, modification-time, alarm-report-control, label, revocation-mode. revocation-mode is auto (default), force-revoked or force-unrevoked. alarm-report-control is allowed (default) or inhibited. id is a string 0..4096; certificate-bytes is PEM, 0..16384 characters; version is v3. To remove a certificate use 'clear certificate'. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration.

Issue 'terminate cable-id' (Operational Mode) to stop all running CableID verification tests; 'show cable-id' lists the cable-id entities. Because verification runs on a port-pair basis, the test can only be stopped after the current port-pair test completes and before the next port-pair starts: a port-pair already under test runs to completion, so the maximum delay to terminate is one port-pair verification time. The test is known to be terminated once cable-id-status cable-id-state changes to idle, so after issuing the command use 'show cable-id cable-id-status' to confirm the entity is back in the idle state. The show form of cable-id also works in Candidate Configuration mode; terminate is Operational Mode only.

The CableID signal can only be sourced or terminated by the CAD10A and RD20TM sleds; the signal is passed transparently through the OPSM. The CableID path starts at the end A port and terminates at the end Z port, where the signal is sourced/terminated, that is at a CAD10A DWDM port or an RD20TM ADE port. In cable-id-path, card-type-a and card-type-z therefore take only the values RD20TM or CAD10A, and port-a/port-z are port AIDs on a CableID-capable sled. These card types are not entered by the operator: they are derived from the provisioned fiber-connection at port-A/port-Z, since when a fiber-connection is created the CableID function checks whether it lands on a port of a CableID capable sled and captures the card type into the CableID path topology. Example: show cable-id-path-1-6-ade3-153-3-dwdm.

Yes. cable-id-status is the container holding the process status and progress of a CableID-based fiber connection verification, and you are allowed to issue 'show cable-id cable-id-status' at any time to query progress. Syntax: 'show cable-id-status [cable-id-state] [test-progress]', usable in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. cable-id-state is idle (verification not running), running-incl-switching (running for both active and protected paths) or running-no-switching (running for the active path only); default idle. test-progress is a string 0..255 characters, default 'None', showing 'Not applicable' if cable-id-state is disabled, or 'N out of M completed' while running, where M is the total number of port-pairs to be tested and N the number completed.

Each carrier can discover up to one node. carrier-neighbor shows a local carrier instance that has discovered that neighbor node, and it is possible for multiple collocated carriers to discover the same node multiple times, each time connected to a different remote carrier. Syntax: 'show carrier-neighbor-<local-carrier> [last-update] [age] [local-carrier-id] [ne-id] [ne-name] [ne-type] [remote-carrier-id] [ipv4-loopback-address] [ipv6-loopback-address]', in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. local-carrier is a string 0..16; ne-id and ne-name are strings 0..256; ne-type and remote-carrier-id are strings 0..64, where remote-carrier-id is the AID of the remote carrier connected to the local carrier and implies a specific remote port id. The loopback addresses may be empty if not configured.

Use 'show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. degree-number is a uint16 in range 1..20 and must be greater than zero and not greater than max-degrees. index is a uint32 in range 1..2, but it is always 1 in the 1830 GX because dwdm-line ports are bi-directional. port-name is an instance-identifier giving the dwdm-line port of the RD or ILAx card; as a consequence the OMS of the corresponding dwdm-port is created. 'show connection-ports*' lists all connection ports in the node (for example connection-ports-1/1 -> port-1-3-dwdm-line1), while 'show connection-ports-5/1' shows a single entry, for example port-name port-4-1-dwdm-line1.

custom-tlv shows the list of Organizational Specific TLV (Type-Length-Value) parameter information. Syntax: 'show custom-tlv-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<oui>/<subtype> [value]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. lldp-port is the local port associated with the LLDP agent, string length 0..64. direction is the direction associated with the LLDP statistics, ingress or egress. oui is the Organization Unique Identifier of the TLV, the hexadecimal representation of the 24-bit identifier, string length 1..6. subtype is the sub-type identifier of the TLV within the scope of that OUI, string length 1..507. The value attribute carries the TLV content.

No. The external-fiber-connection is set autonomously by TNMS; although it is possible to configure it manually, it is not recommended to do so. The object is the physical link representation of a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations. Syntax: 'add external-fiber-connection-<name> src-port-name <value> dst-port-name <value> [label] [scope] [src-node-id] [src-card-name] [dst-node-id] [dst-card-name] [fiber-connection-type]', plus set (label only), show and delete. Before R8.0 the operator also had to set port external-connectivity to yes. scope is general-purpose (default) or cable-id, and entries representing intra-NE RD20TM ADE to ADE or CAD10A DWDM to RD20TM ADE links must use cable-id. fiber-connection-type is one-way or two-way, default two-way.

fiber-connection is the physical link representation of a connection between two distinct ports (or two distinct sub-ports) in the same NE, used in an OADM/ILA topology: 'add|set fiber-connection-<name> [label] [src-port] [dst-port] [fiber-connection-type]', plus show and delete; src-port and dst-port are instance identifiers, name is 0..64 characters, label 0..256, fiber-connection-type is one-way or two-way with default two-way. external-fiber-connection is the physical link representation of a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations; it identifies endpoints by src-node-id/src-card-name/src-port-name and dst-node-id/dst-card-name/dst-port-name strings, carries a scope attribute (general-purpose or cable-id) and is normally set autonomously by TNMS.

Yes. icdp is the Nokia Carrier Discovery Protocol, and its single attribute global-switch is a flag to enable icdp with values true or false and a default of true, so the protocol is on unless it has been turned off. Commands: 'set icdp global-switch <true|false>' and 'show icdp [global-switch]', both available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The icdp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: set icdp global-switch true.

INCI is the Inter-NE Communication Interface, an API-based communication infrastructure for control plane communication across different network elements, for example between a transponder such as CHM6 on 1830 GX G40 and a line system such as FLEXILS. It uses gRPC server/client as the core mechanism: when the INCI service is enabled the gRPC server starts and binds to the local IP address, and when an INCI neighbor instance is configured gRPC client sessions are established. The switch is inci-enabled, values true or false, default false, so INCI is not running by default. Commands: 'set inci [inci-enabled <true|false>]' and 'show inci [inci-enabled]' in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Enable with: set inci inci-enabled true.

Compare the configured-node-name you provisioned against the discovered-node-name reported by the far end. On 'add inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id> neighbor-address <value> configured-node-name <value> [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>]' the configured-node-name is the user-provisioned name of the remote NE, string 0..128, explicitly used to compare against the discovered-node-name. 'show inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id> [neighbor-address] [neighbor-port] [connection-status] [configured-node-name] [discovered-node-name] [discovered-node-id] [alarm-report-control] [oper-state]' returns discovered-node-name (name of the remote NE as sent by the remote NE, string 0..128) and discovered-node-id (node ID received from the remote node, string 0..12). oper-state is enabled or disabled; alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited.

Both timers are attributes of interface-neighbor: 'set interface-neighbor-<local-interface> [discovery-cycle-time <value>] [discovery-timeout <value>] [discovery-enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]'. discovery-cycle-time is the periodicity at which sndp discover messages are sent, range 30..300 seconds, default 30. discovery-timeout is the time after which discovery is considered failed, range 300..1800 seconds, default 300; when this timeout occurs the neighbor-adjacency-state transitions to blackout. discovery-enabled (true/false, default true) switches discovery on the local interface. neighbor-adjacency-state can be blackout, discovery, holding or unknown (default unknown). Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration.

No. 'show links' displays the links container within the topology, and these links are dynamically filled in by the system, allowing the NCT topology to be derived and displayed. The command takes no parameters and is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The same applies to nct-connection, which shows the existing links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE and is likewise dynamically filled in by the system.

The retention time is the LLDP hold-on-timer, set with 'set lldp [hold-on-timer <value>]' and read with 'show lldp [hold-on-timer]', both available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. It is the time to keep neighbor information in the case where the neighbor does not supply an explicit Time-To-Live (TTL) TLV; the value is a number of seconds and the default is 900. The lldp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Per-neighbor, the lldp-neighbor ttl attribute gives the number of seconds until the remote system information expires, and if the remote system does not provide a ttl value that parameter is set to the global hold-on-timer. Example: set lldp hold-on-timer 60.

Use 'show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> [chassis-id-subtype] [chassis-id] [port-id-subtype] [port-id] [port-description] [system-name] [system-description] [supported-capabilities] [enabled-capabilities]' to see the LLDP local system information sent on an lldp-port. On the 1830 GX: chassis-id-subtype is chassis-component and chassis-id is the chassis serial number; port-id-subtype is local and port-id is the port AID; port-description is the port name; system-name is the NE name; and system-description is the string 'Nokia Corporation.Converged OS, Version <release id> build <software label>'. All these strings are 0..255 characters. supported-capabilities and enabled-capabilities take router and bridge. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration. Examples: show lldp-local-info, show lldp-local-info-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4.

No. For lldp-neighbor the egress direction is not supported: in 'show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/<direction> ...' the direction parameter, which is the direction in which the neighbor was detected, has only the value ingress. The same restriction applies to lldp-port-statistics. lldp-neighbor shows the LLDP remote system discovered by the lldp-port and returns last-update, age, chassis-id-subtype, chassis-id, port-id-subtype, port-id, port-description, system-name, system-description, supported-capabilities, enabled-capabilities and ttl. This information is kept indefinitely until the port is decommissioned or the data is manually cleared by the user. Examples: show -r lldp-neighbor, show -r lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-1-3/ingress.

No. All counter values in a particular lldp-port-statistics entry are maintained on a continuing basis and are not deleted upon expiration of the TTL timing counters associated with the LLDP neighbor information. The counters do freeze: all statistical counters associated with a port on the local LLDP agent become frozen whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled for that port. Syntax: 'show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/<direction> [last-change-time] [last-clear-time] [total-ageouts] [total-discarded-frames] [error-frames] [total-frames-in] [total-frames-out] [total-discarded-tlvs] [total-unrecognized-tlvs]'; direction is ingress only, the egress direction is not supported. total-ageout counts the times a neighbor's information was deleted from the lldp-neighbor list due to TTL expiry; counters default to 0 and last-clear-time defaults to 0000-01-01T00:00:00Z.

Use 'show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> [src-chassis] [dst-chassis] [src-chassis-state] [dst-chassis-state]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. It shows NCT connectivity information, the existing links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE, dynamically filled in by the system so the NCT topology can be derived. src-chassis-state and dst-chassis-state take the values node controller, provisioned and unprovisioned. src-port and dst-port must be NCT ports: for a commissioned chassis the port AID is used, and for an unprovisioned chassis the format is '<chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>'. Likewise src-chassis/dst-chassis is the chassis AID when commissioned and the chassis serial number when unprovisioned; all four are strings 0..64. Example row: nct-connection-1-1-NCT-1/254-1-NCT-2, chassis 1 node-controller, chassis 254 provisioned.

sndp has a single attribute, sndp-enabled, which is the switch controlling the sndp feature. Values are true or false and the default is true. Commands: 'set sndp [sndp-enabled <value>]' and 'show sndp [sndp-enabled]', both available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show sndp sndp-enabled. The protocol is what drives interface neighbor discovery: interface-neighbor discovery-cycle-time is the periodicity at which sndp discover messages are sent (30..300 seconds, default 30).

Add with 'add submarine-link-<name> src-node-id <value> src-port-name <value> dst-node-id <value> dst-port-name <value> degree-target-tx-power <value> [label] [src-card-name] [dst-card-name] [fiber-connection-type] [link-name] [fiber-pair-id] [fiber-length] [segment-list] [bu-segment-index] [rx-fiber-type] [tx-fiber-type] [gsnr] [degree-expected-rx-power] [commissioning-snr-margin] [launch-condition] [allocated-spectrum-list]'; set, show and delete also exist. Mandatory are src-node-id, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-port-name (the NE names and the OTS dwdm-line ports of the degrees) and degree-target-tx-power. fiber-length is a decimal64 in the range 0..25000 km, default 0, and excludes branch segment length. fiber-connection-type is two-way (default) or one-way, and is two-way only for submarine links. launch-condition is flat-tx or pfib, default pfib. bu-segment-index is uint16, default 0. allocated-spectrum-list holds max 32 start/end frequency elements.

supporting-fiber-connection shows the list of fiber connections that support a path. Syntax: 'show supporting-fiber-connection-<name> [fiber-connection-list]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. name is the entity name, a string 0..64 characters; fiber-connection-list is an instance-identifier giving the supported fiber connection path. It is the container reported for a CableID path: in cable-id-path, supporting-fiber-connection is the container holding fiber-connection-list and it is displayed when the -r flag is used, as in 'show -r cable-id-path-1-6-ade6-1-8-ade6', which returns supporting-fiber-connection-1-6-ade6-1-8-ade6 with fiber-connection-list supporting-fiber-connection-R1.

Use `clear [-f] topology [target=]<value>`. The target is an instance-identifier and may be an lldp-neighbor instance (discovered via LLDP), a carrier-neighbor instance (discovered via ICMP), or an lldp-port-statistics instance (details associated with an LLDP enabled port). Clearing manually removes the existing topology neighbor information. Use `clear topology <tab>` to list the valid topology objects, and the -f flag to force the command without the confirmation prompt. Example: `clear topology lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-4-T1-1`. The paired `show topology` command retrieves topology information and accepts inci, links, lldp, icdp or sndp. Access mode is Operational Mode; Candidate Configuration Mode is allowed for the show command only.

Use `verify [-f] [type-select=]<value> [[target-select=]<value>] [allow-switching]`, for example `verify fiber-connection port-1-6-ade11`. type-select currently supports only fiber-connection. target-select is the port instance-identifier of the CableID-capable card; if omitted, all paths are verified. If the port is in multiple CableID paths, all of them are checked. allow-switching (true/false, default false) decides whether verification may initiate switching on the OPSM: true includes active and inactive paths (system initiated switching), false covers active paths only, so it does not disturb an in-service system. Pre-condition: equipment-policies cable-id-control must be enabled. The command prompts for confirmation (-f skips it), raises the CID-verification-in-progress alarm against the NE until all queued requests finish, and is non-blocking; check progress with `show cable-id-status`.

Use the `bert` command in Operational Mode: `bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=ingress test-duration=10`, then `bert stop test-id=TestX` to stop or abort an in-progress test. test-id is mandatory for stop; if not given on start the system generates a unique one (alphanumeric [A-Z][a-z][0-9]). test-signal-type: none (default), PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV, scrambled-idles; 100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles, ODU4 uses PRBS31/PRBS31NONINV. Monitoring type adds fec-frames (CarrierCTP). Directions are ingress/egress. test-duration is in seconds, min 10 up to 1000 hrs; 0 (default) means indefinite. Also available: `bert get` and `bert delete` by test-id, resource or AID. Multiple simultaneous BERTs can run on a facility if each meets the pre-conditions.

The cid-ptp facility is system created: it is created automatically when a card supporting the CableID function is created, for example RD20TM or CAD10A. There is no user creation, managed-by is system, and only user-created facilities can be user deleted. The facility supports the CableID SFP and its connection to the card via the CID port. Only `set cid-ptp-<name> [label] [admin-state]` and `show cid-ptp-<name>` are available. admin-state is not editable, the only supported value is unlock, and CableID operation is not affected by the cid-ptp admin-state. The read-only `used` attribute (true/false, default false) is true when CableID functionality is supported. Example: `show cid-ptp-1-4-spcid` on an RD20TM SPCID port, or `show cid-ptp-1-6-spu` on a CAD10A SPU port.

The Digital Coherent 400ZR eth-zr facility is auto-instantiated when the ZR TOM is provisioned; interface-type shows 400ZR (Media-interface 400ZR-CFEC-DP-16QAM) and rate is 400.000 Gbit/s. fec-type is settable with values not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4 (EFEC-I4), i7 (EFEC-I7), sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 (7% HDFEC Staircase) and ufec7 (7% UFEC); the default is ofec, and a 400ZR TOM typically reports cfec. Degrade monitoring uses two pairs: FEC Detected Degrade with fdd-monitoring (enabled/disabled, default disabled), fdd-threshold (default 0.0195 avg BER) and fdd-clear-threshold (default 0.01062), and FEC Excessive Degrade with fed-monitoring (default disabled), fed-threshold (default 0.0206) and fed-clear-threshold (default 0.01125). All four thresholds are decimal64(9) in the range 0.000000001..0.1 average BER. Example: `set eth-zr-1-6-T8 fed-threshold 0.011870000`.

The largest frame is governed by the ethernet facility attribute max-packet-length, the maximum transfer unit in octets, set with `set ethernet-<name> max-packet-length <value>`. The range is 1280..18000 octets on the 1830 GX G30 and 1518..18000 octets on the 1830 GX G40; the default in both cases is 1518. Two restrictions apply: the parameter is configurable at card level only and applies to all interfaces on that card, and it is used only for determining the undersized/oversized packet counts in 100GbE PMs. The value is readable with `show ethernet-<name> max-packet-length`. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show facilities`. It is a display-only command that shows the system facilities configured on the node; it takes no parameters and has no set/add form. Access is allowed in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The output is a flat list of every provisioned facility instance by name, for example on a 1830 GX G40 node: super-channel-group-1-4-L1, super-channel-1-4-L1-1, optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1, optical-channel-1-4-L1-1, trib-ptp-1-4-T11, comm-channel-1-4-L1-1, otu-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni, otu-1-4-T11, ethernet-1-4-T2, odu-1-4-L1-1-ODUCni, odu-1-4-L2-1-ODUflexi-1 and odu-1-4-T11. The names listed are the instance identifiers you then pass to the per-facility show and set commands.

The `fc` facility (set/show only) carries two Fibre Channel specific attributes for the 32GFC client: tts, which enables or disables Transmitter Training Signal support, with values enabled/disabled and a default of disabled; and laser-toggling-for-tts, which enables or disables laser toggling when tts is enabled/disabled for the 32GFC client, values enabled/disabled with a default of enabled. Set them with `set fc-<name> [tts <value>] [laser-toggling-for-tts <value>]`. The read-only fc-type reports the signal type: FC1G, FC2G, FC4G, FC8G, FC16G or FC32G. Other configurable attributes are label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control, tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode (GMP default), loopback, loopback-mode, test-signal-type, test-signal-direction (default ingress) and test-signal-monitoring.

The read-only foic-type on the flexo facility gives the interface type. FOICx.k means k parallel lanes carrying a FlexO-x interface, where order x is the rate in units of 100G, per G.709.3 FlexO-LR and G.709.1 FlexO-SR. The supported values are foic1.2, foic1.4, foic2.4, foic2.8, foic3.6, foic4.8 and foic4.16, with foic4.8 as the default. fec-type is also read-only: not-applicable, cfec, ofec or noFEC, default ofec. resource-mode is the settable attribute and selects the resource mode of the interface: ADM for add-drop, or XC for add-drop with regen. The default is ADM. Set it with, for example, `set flexo-1-5-L1-1 resource-mode 'XC'`. Other settable attributes are label, admin-state, alarm-report-control, iid and the fdd/fed raise and clear thresholds.

Creation requires four mandatory attributes: `add flexo-group-<name> carriers <value> rate <value> modulation-format <value> group-id <value>`. carriers is the list of carriers bound to the facility, a string of length 1..32. rate is the carried signal basic rate class in Gbit/s. modulation-format is one of not-applicable, DP-QPSK, DP-16QAM, DP-8QAM or BPSK. group-id indicates the interface group instance that the FlexO-x interface is a member of and must be unique in the NE, an integer in the range 1..1048575. Optional on add are label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed) and fec-type (not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7, ufec7; default ofec). `set` additionally accepts expected-gid, flexo-type, loopback and loopback-mode. Access mode is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

high-speed-monitoring is a node-level object with just two attributes, managed with `set high-speed-monitoring [enabled <value>] [port <value>]` and `show high-speed-monitoring [enabled] [port]`. enabled is the user configurable switch that turns high speed monitoring on or off, with values true or false and a default of false. port is the user configurable port used for high speed monitoring, a uint16 in the range [1..max], with a default of 57500. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The interlaken facility represents the SPN2 Interlaken interface. Its capacity attribute is read-only, showing the total capacity of the interface as 500 Gbit/s (the only value and the default). The facility is always system created (managed-by system), and supporting-port shows the paired ports, for example 8,9 with supporting-facilities trib-ptp-66-1-8,trib-ptp-66-1-9. Only four attributes are settable via `set interlaken-<name>`: label (string 0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and loopback (none, facility or terminal; default none, where facility tests towards the facility side and terminal towards the terminal side). Example: `set interlaken-66-1-8 label interlaken_66_1`. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Auto-in-service on a line-ptp is driven by two attributes on `add`/`set line-ptp-<name>`. auto-in-service-enabled is the auto-in-service switch for the facility, values true or false, default false. valid-signal-time is the configurable time that represents detection of a valid signal and is used by the auto-in-service mechanism; it is a number in the range 1..7200 minutes with a default of 480. The read-only remaining-valid-signal-time (also 1..7200 minutes) shows the actual time still to run before the facility is automatically enabled by the auto-in-service mechanism. While waiting, the facility reports avail-state auto-in-service. Example output: auto-in-service-enabled false, valid-signal-time 480 minutes, remaining-valid-signal-time 0 minutes. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

They are different commands. `show network-xconnect` is a display-only command with no parameters that lists the services of the multiple user cross connections commissioned in this NE. nw-xconnect is the object itself: `add nw-xconnect-<name> endpoint1 <value> endpoint2 <value> [xcon-type <value>] [rate <value>]`, plus `set nw-xconnect-<name> [rate <value>]`, `show nw-xconnect-<name> [AID] [oper-state] [avail-state] [endpoint1] [endpoint2] [xcon-type] [rate]` and `delete nw-xconnect-<name>`. So network-xconnect gives the list view of what is commissioned, while nw-xconnect creates, modifies, inspects and deletes an individual user channel cross-connection. Both run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Create an nw-xconnect user channel cross-connection. xcon-type selects the bridge: L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 (L1-ETH to GCC0), L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0 (GCC0 to GCC0, the default), L1-ETH-TO-OSC (L1-ETH to OSC) and L1-OSC-TO-OSC. For GCC to OSC bridging via the management Ethernet, first set the port with `set comm-eth-1-12-ETH4 mode L1`, then for example `add nw-xconnect-test xcon-type L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 endpoint1 comm-eth-1-12-ETH4 endpoint2 comm-channel-ch1`, or `add nw-xconnect-test1 xcon-type L1-ETH-TO-OSC endpoint1 comm-eth-1-16-ETH4 endpoint2 comm-channel-1-6-dwdm-line-OSCX5`. endpoint1 and endpoint2 are mandatory instance-identifiers: comm-eth for the ETH end, a GCC0 comm-channel or an OSCX-5 comm-channel as appropriate. rate is the maximum bandwidth of the user channel, uint8 range 1..20 Mbps, default 13 for L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 and 20 for L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC. Remove with `delete nw-xconnect-<name>`.

No. The high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created. When a CHM6 has an OTU configured on it, use the `show odu` command to determine whether the ODU already exists. What you create yourself are the low order ODUs, the ODU4i (100G) or ODUflexi (400G) facilities that XCONs are mapped into, with `add odu-<name> odu-type <value> ...`; the pre-condition is that the super-channel must be added before low order ODUs can be added. The read-only class attribute reflects this: high-order marks the top-most ODUCn/ODUk entity created by the system, low-order (the default) marks children supported by a high-order ODU, and mapped marks a mapped client signal; the system sets it based on the order of creation.
