Example: `add odu-1-1 odu-type ODU4i parent-odu '1-7-L1-1-ODUCni' time-slots 1..80`.

Yes. odu-diagnostics is keyed per direction: the object name is `odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction>` where direction is ingress or egress, and each direction has its own values. Use `add`/`set odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction>` with tx-tti, expected-tti, and the ITU split fields expected-sapi, expected-dapi, expected-operator, tx-sapi, tx-dapi and tx-operator. tti-style selects the format: ITU-T-G709 (default), which splits the TTI into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes, or proprietary, a single 64 byte string. tx-tti and expected-tti accept a hex string with '0x' prefix (length 1..130) or printable ASCII up to 64 characters; SAPI and DAPI are up to 15 characters (hex up to 32) and operator up to 32 characters (hex up to 66). Defaults for the expected/tx fields are the empty string. Example: `set odu-diagnostics-Lodu4i/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPIDAPI-OPER`.

Yes, FEC is on by default. On the otu facility fec-mode, the configured Forward Error Correction mode on the OTUk/OTUCn client, takes enabled or disabled and defaults to enabled. fec-generation-mode, the configured FEC generation mode towards the far-end receiver, likewise takes enabled or disabled and defaults to enabled. fec-type selects the FEC used, with values not-applicable, cfec, ofec, G709, noFEC, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 and ufec7; the default is ofec. All three are available on add, set and show, for example `set otu-<name> fec-mode enabled fec-type ofec`. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Set tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting on the otu-diagnostics object for the direction you care about: `set otu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI`, for example `set otu-diagnostics-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI`. The attribute indicates whether the TTI-Mismatch (TIM) alarm is reported or masked and, if reported, the criteria used. Values are disabled (the default, alarm masked), full-64-bytes, SAPI, DAPI, OPER, SAPI_DAPI, SAPI_OPER, DAPI_OPER and SAPI_DAPI_OPER. So choosing SAPI alarms only on a mismatched Source Access Point Identifier rather than the whole 64-byte trace. This requires tti-style ITU-T-G709 (the default), which splits the TTI into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes; proprietary style treats the TTI as a single 64 byte string. Separately, tim-act-enabled (enabled/disabled, default disabled) decides whether a maintenance signal is inserted on TIM.

The stm facility handles the Synchronous Transport Module N (STM-N) per ITU-T G.691. The read-only stm-type attribute reports the type of SDH signal and its permitted values are STM-16 and STM-64, so those are the SDH rates terminated. Related service-type values on trib-ptp are STM16 and STM64. The stm object supports set and show only: settable attributes are label, admin-state (Lock, Unlock, Maintenance; default Unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), tx-mapping-mode, expected-mapping-mode, tti-style (ITU-T-G709 default, or proprietary), tim-monitor (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tx-tti, expected-tti, loopback, loopback-mode (none, facility, terminal; default none), test-signal-type (none default, PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31), test-signal-direction (Ingress) and test-signal-monitoring. Example: `set stm-1-5-T9.2 tx-mapping-mode BMP`.

The behaviour is set by tributary-disable-action on the trib-ptp facility: it indicates what action the NE performs towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, either shutting off the laser or inserting a replacement signal. Values are laser-shut-off (the default), none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais, and send-nos for 1830 GX G30 only. Example: `set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off`. tributary-disable-holdoff-timer is the hold off time for client shutdown or replacement signal in the egress direction, uint16 range 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 meaning holdoff is disabled; it applies only when the TDA action is laser-turnoff. Related: near-end-tda (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tda-degrade-mode (default disabled) and forward-defect-trigger (true/false, default true).

Create a Layer 1 digital service with `add xcon-<name> source <value> destination <value> [payload-type <value>] [direction <value>] [label <value>] [circuit-id-suffix <value>]`, for example `add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1` on a G40, or `add xcon-11 source odu-1-1-3-ODU4 destination odu-1-1-1-ODU4-1` on a G30. source and destination are instance IDs; direction supports only two-way, which is also the default. Only label and circuit-id-suffix (string 0..48) can be changed with `set`; remove with `delete xcon-<name>`. protection-type is read-only and represents the protection this XCON has: y-cable, snc-n, snc-i or unprotected, with unprotected as the default. Other read-only views include payload-type (100GBE, 400GBE, OTU4, 100G, ODU2, ODU2e, empty), payload-treatment, network-mapping, type (add, drop, add-drop, express) and managed-by (default user).

The L2-bridge object is identified by bridge-name, which is part of the command name itself: `set L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name <value>] [description <value>]` and `show L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name] [description]`. bridge-name is a string of length 0..64. There are only two configurable attributes: chassis-name, a leafref giving the chassis associated with this L2 bridge, and description, a string of length 0..255 describing the bridge and its intended purpose. Both default to n/a and are available on set and show. Only set and show are offered; there is no add or delete form. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use the `clear app` command, which clears third party apps: `clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>`. The app-name parameter is the third party app name. The -f flag forces the command to run without a confirmation prompt. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. To control rather than remove an application, use `appctl` instead, which supports the restart, netls and exec commands.

Use `appctl [app-name=]<value> [command=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[parameters=]<value>[,<value>]*]`. app-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:sw-management/ioa-ne:third-party-app/ioa-ne:app-name. command is one of restart (restarts the third party application), netls (shows the list of subnet networks used by the containers) or exec (executes a third party application operation given in parameters). target says where the command is executed, either the string system or a chassis/card AID; the default is system. parameters are optional values passed with the command, with max-elements 50, applicable when command is restart or exec. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. To remove an app instead, use `clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>`.

Yes. Use the call-home command: `call-home [dial-out-server-name=]<string>`. It executes a manual connection trigger to a configured dial-out-server, forcing a connection attempt. If the dial-out-server is currently in the 'connecting' state, call-home forces an immediate attempt and will not wait for some time before retrying. The dial-out-server-name parameter is the pre-configured name of the dial-out server (string, no default). Access Mode is Operational Mode, and the pre-condition is that the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly. Examples: `call-home collector-x`, `call-home dialoutservername`, and `call-home -h` for help.

Use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` with attributes [related-session-id] [related-dial-out-server] [session-type] [session-protocol] [encoding] [transfer-mode] [updates-only] [user-access]. The encoding attribute specifies the data encoding scheme for data sent to and from the target device; permitted values are json, bytes, proto, ascii and json-ietf, default json-ietf. The encoding may be specified for all data or optionally per-RPC if the target supports it. transfer-mode specifies the data transfer mode to the target: stream (values streamed by the target), once (values sent once-off) and poll (values sent in response to a poll request), default stream. session-protocol is gnmi (default gnmi). Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

No, YANG data models are not all loaded by default: the data-model 'enabled' attribute defaults to false. Use `set data-model-<name> enabled <value>` with true or false to load/unload a model; a loaded data model means it can be used via the management interfaces. Use `show data-model-<name> [description] [enabled]` to view attributes, or `show data-model` to list all available YANG data models for loading/unloading. The name is the model name, String (length 0..256); description is the data model description, String (length 0..256), show only. Access Mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode.

The dial-out-server retry-policy attribute takes progressive-back-off, retry-then-stop or retry-forever, defaulting to progressive-back-off. The retry attribute (Integer, range 0..5, default 3) is the number of retries and applies only when retry-policy is retry-then-stop. The timeout attribute is the timeout before next retry, Integer range 1..255 seconds, default 10; it is not applicable for progressive-back-off, which has a dynamic timeout. The port is the dial-out-server session port, Integer range 1..65535, default 4334 (the default for netconf protocol over ssh). protocol is netconf or restconf, default netconf; transport is ssh. Example: `set dial-out-server-callhome1 retry-policy retry-then-stop port 4889 timeout 200 retry 5`.

Yes, gRPC/gNMI is enabled by default: the grpc 'enabled' attribute defaults to true. The port that listens for gNMI access via gRPC when gRPC is enabled defaults to 50051. Use `show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity]` to view and `set grpc [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity <value>]` to change, for example `set grpc enabled false`. The gnmi-get-encoding-granularity attribute controls the granularity of data in JSON-encoded gNMI Get responses: per-path puts all path data in one Update message, per-object divides path data into multiple Update messages, one per YANG container/list entry; default per-object. The grpc object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

NETCONF listens for access via ssh on port 830 by default (port-number, uint16, range 1..65535). The hello-timeout attribute specifies the number of seconds a session may exist before the hello PDU is received/transmitted; a session is dropped if no hello PDU is received/transmitted before that many seconds elapse. Range is 1..3600 seconds, default 2. Use `show netconf [enabled] [port] [annotate-cli-name] [static-info-in-notifs] [hello-timeout]` and `set netconf [...]`. NETCONF is enabled by default (enabled=true) and it is not possible to disable NETCONF from within a NETCONF session. Access Mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode.

RESTCONF itself is enabled by default (enabled=true), but plain HTTP is not: http-enabled defaults to false, and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. https-enabled defaults to true. The http-port default is 8080 and the https-port default is 8181, both in range 1..65535. Session lifetime is governed by cookie-timeout, the timeout of a cookie based RESTCONF session, range 1..300 minutes, default 5; the cookie expiration date is reset every time there is activity on the session. Example: `set restconf cookie-timeout 10`. show also exposes api-root, the root of the RESTCONF API (String, length 0..64).

Use `show snmp [enabled] [port] [snmp-engine-id] [engine-boot-count]`. snmp-engine-id is the SNMP EngineID of the NE, a show-only String (length 0..256); it follows the EngineID format 3 defined in RFC3411, and the MAC address in the Engine ID is the first MAC address of the MAC addresses Pool of the NE. engine-boot-count is also show-only, a uint16 counting how many times the engine has restarted, default 0. The settable attributes are enabled (true/false, default true, global SNMP access) and port (range 1..65535, default 161, where the NE listens for SNMP requests). Note the trap-community-string lives in the snmp-target object.

No. The snmp-community attribute community-string-access, the SNMP access right of the community string, has read-only as its only permitted value and read-only as its default. Create a community with `add snmp-community-<name> community-string <value> [enabled <value>] [community-string-access <value>]`, where name is the name for the community (different from the community string itself, String length 0..64) and community-string is the community string itself (String length 1..32). enabled defaults to true. Example: `add snmp-community-mycommunity community-string public community-string-access read-only enabled true`. Related commands are add snmp-target and add snmpv3-user; the trap-community-string is in the snmp-target object.

Add a trap listener with `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]`. snmp-version is v2c or v3, default v2c. trap-community-string is the community string used for SNMP traps, String (0...32), default infinera. target-port is the UDP port number, range 0..65535, default 162, and target-transport is udp (default udp). enabled defaults to true. target-name is String (0...32); target-address is an IPv4 or IPv6 address or hostname, optionally with a %-separated zone index. snmpv3-user applies only when snmp-version is v3.

A new SNMPv3 user gets user-sec-level no-auth-no-priv by default; the permitted values are auth-no-priv, auth-priv and no-auth-no-priv. The privacy protocol priv-protocol supports DES, AES128, AES192 and AES256, default AES128. The only authentication protocol is SHA (default SHA). Create with `add snmpv3-user-<snmpv3-user-name> auth-passphrase <value> priv-passphrase <value> [user-sec-level <value>] [auth-protocol <value>] [priv-protocol <value>]`; the user name is String length 1...32 and both passphrases are String length 8...64. Example: `add snmpv3-user-bob user-sec-level auth-priv auth-protocol SHA auth-passphrase public123 priv-protocol AES128 priv-passphrase private123`.

The subscription-path-mode attribute controls how subscription updates are sent: target-defined, on-change or sample, default target-defined. View it with `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name> [subscription-path] [subscription-path-origin] [subscription-path-mode] [sample-interval] [heartbeat-interval] [suppress-redundant]`. sample-interval is the time in milliseconds between samples of a telemetry data source, default 0 (set to 0 when optional); for a target-defined stream subscription, if sample-interval is not set the system automatically adjusts it from 0 to 10 seconds. heartbeat-interval (milliseconds, default 0) is the maximum interval that may pass between updates; if sample-interval is not set and heartbeat-interval is below 10 seconds, the system adjusts it to 20 seconds. suppress-redundant (true/false, default true) suppresses redundant updates.

Use `show subscriptions`. It shows a list of subscriptions and takes no parameters. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For a list representation of the telemetry subscriptions configured in the system, use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` with attributes such as [related-session-id] [related-dial-out-server] [session-type] [session-protocol] [encoding] [transfer-mode] [updates-only] [user-access]. For per-path detail use `show subscription-path` or `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>`.

Telemetry is configured through the telemetry command: `show telemetry` and `set telemetry id <string>`. The command configures persistent and dynamic telemetry, and the object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Its single parameter id is described as persistent and dynamic telemetry, string of length 0..4096, with no default. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `show telemetry` to view the telemetry subscription. Individual subscriptions are inspected with `show subscriptions`, `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` and `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>`.

Use `show third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable]`, or `show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> [version] [state] [information]`. The state attribute reports running, stopped or failed, with stopped as the default. The enable attribute is the third-party-app enabled state: true or false, default false, so apps are not enabled by default. If enabled, the app is started and stays enabled upon system restart; if disabled, the app is stopped. Other attributes: version (string 0..64), vendor (string 0..64), product (string 0..256), information (string 0..1024). Change them with `set third-party-app-<app-name> ...`. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `add <tab>` to visualize all entity types that are creatable at that time. The add command creates a new managed entity in the system database: `add [-v|-m|-f] <entity id> [(<attribute> <value>) ...]`. Some entities have mandatory attributes that must be provided upon creation; if a mandatory attribute is not given in the command itself, the CLI automatically asks for it. Non-mandatory attributes can also be initialized with attribute-value pairs. Entities managed by the system cannot be created with add. Flags: -h help, -v validates the command only (entity not created, replies 'OK' if valid), -m merge (best effort add: creates if absent, updates with the supplied attributes if present), -f forces without confirmation. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration.

Yes, in all cases the clear command requires a user confirmation, and a confirmation prompt is displayed if the -f flag is not provided. Use `clear -f ...` to force the command without confirmation; -h displays help. clear clears entries for the specified entity, and each sub command handles a specific type of clear operation. Sub commands are alarm, app, certificate, crl, database, dns, file, isk, log, ospf, pm, recover-mode, statistics, system and topology. Access Mode is Operational Mode. Note that `clear system factory-reset` with the shutdown option is not supported on the L0 cards.

Yes, via the cli object's show-alarm-columns attribute, which sets the columns displayed in the output of the 'show alarm' CLI command. Permitted values are a list of columns separated by a comma, default-columns (the pre-defined columns), or default-columns,<additional-details> to add the <additional-details> column to the pre-defined ones. The default is default-columns. This configuration has a global effect and takes effect on all CLI sessions. Examples: `set cli show-alarm-columns col1,col2,col3` and `set cli show-alarm-columns default-columns,corrective-action`. Other cli attributes are enabled (default true; CLI cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port (range 1..65535, default 22), script-dir (show only) and default-interactive-mode (default true).

Use `set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value>`. cli-lines is the configurable number of rows used for display before pausing the output; range 10..1000, default 40. After pausing, pressing [SPACEBAR] resumes the display. Width is set with cli-columns, the number of columns used for display, range 80..4000, default 80. The same object also carries interactive-mode (true/false, default true; set per CLI session and not persistent) and display-timestamp (true/false, default false). Examples: `set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-lines 30` and `set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-columns 100`; `show cli-session-config-<session-id>` shows all attributes.

Yes. The connect command establishes an ssh session directly from the CLI: `connect [target-address=]<value> [user-name=]<value> [[port=]<value>]`. target-address may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or hostname (if DNS is configured); it requires connectivity and is a mandatory attribute. user-name is a string of 0..64 characters. port is optional: by default port 22 is used, but another port can be provided if needed, which is useful to access the shell port. Access Mode is Operational Mode. Example: `connect 10.41.24.55 admin port=8022`, which then prompts for the password for that user on the target.

Yes, use `convert [target-representation=]<value> [command=]<value>`. target-representation accepts netconf-xml (an entire NETCONF xml payload), netconf-python (Python code performing a NETCONF request), restconf-json (HTTP method, URI, headers and body with JSON payloads), restconf-xml (same with XML payloads), restconf-python, plaintext-to-encrypted (encrypts a string based on security-policies/csp-passphrase), snmp-oids (OIDs for objects in a 'show' command) and netsnmp-cmd (a shell command performing an SNMP request). The command should be enclosed in quotes; multiple commands separated by ';' are merged into one payload where possible. Generated Python works with Python 2 or 3 and needs ncclient for NETCONF or requests for RESTCONF; host, IP and user-name are auto filled, only the password must be entered. Example: `convert restconf-python 'ping 1.23.151.23'`.

No. The default command assigns default values to the targeted entities, but some configuration attributes will not be reset to default, including mandatory parameters and attributes only settable at creation. Syntax: `default [-f] [entity-id=][,]* [[attribute=][,]*]`. If attributes are specified only those are set to their default value; otherwise all possible configuration attributes are defaulted. Multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*), for example `default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/*` or `default alarm-severity-entry-*`; `default tom-1-4-T16 label,phy-mode` defaults just those two attributes. Flags: -h help, -f forces without confirmation. The default command is not supported in 1830 GX G30 Releases 5.0 and 5.1.

Use the -b flag: `delete -b <entity-id>`. Starting from R9.0 the best effort delete only bypasses the check for object existence, so it does not fail and displays no error if the object does not exist, whereas standard `delete <object>` fails when the object is absent. The -b option may still produce other errors, such as precondition failures, and delete -b has the same functionality as a NETCONF 'remove' operation. Full syntax is `delete [-f|-v|-b] <entity-id> [<filter> ...]`; -f forces without the confirmation prompt, -v validates only and replies 'OK' if valid. Deleting an entity removes it and all sub-level objects, and is not allowed if it or its sub-level containers carry services or other traffic affecting configurations.

The exit command logs out of the current CLI mode: it terminates the current CLI session if you are in operational mode, or leaves configuration mode if you are in candidate mode. A confirmation prompt is displayed unless the -f flag is provided. Syntax is `exit [-h|-f]`, where -h displays help and -f forces the command without confirmation. The keyboard shortcut Ctrl+D has the same effect as `exit -f`, so it leaves the mode straight away with no confirmation. Access Mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use the expect command: `expect [-r] [<instance>=]<value> [<expected-value>=]<value> [<attribute>=]<value>`. It validates an existing attribute value against an expected value; if the value matches, no output is seen, and if it does not, an ERROR message is shown. It is intended for scripts and automation to guarantee specific assumptions and can be invoked multiple times to validate multiple attributes; a common use is validating system details at the start of a script. If the script runs in 'stop-on-error' mode, a failed expect stops the script immediately. Wildcards to select multiple object instances or attributes are not supported. The -r flag enables regex mode, making the expected-value a regular expression instead of a literal string. Examples: `expect ne ne-name GX-NE-123` and `expect -r software-load-active swload-version R5.*`.

Yes. The `export` command defines variables for use in CLI, referenced as ${variable} in any CLI command. Syntax: `export [-h]` and `export [<variable>=[<value>]]`. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The variable name can be any alphanumeric string; the value can be any supported character, including spaces. Variables do NOT survive logout: they are locally defined per session and are removed after the session is closed. This makes them mainly useful inside CLI scripts. Declare with `export SLOT_NUMBER=2`, delete by assigning nothing (`export SLOT_NUMBER=`), and list all existing variables by typing `export` on its own, which prints entries such as `export MYSESSIONID="10.100.152.29:56154"` and `export MYUSERNAME="admin"`.

Both launch a Linux bash shell from within the CLI and both run in Operational Mode, but they target different environments. `shell [-h] [shell command]` launches the shell on the node itself, using the currently logged in user and allowing only commands accessible to that user; certain commands can be run with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo' (permitted list includes /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and several /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts). `gshell [-h] [<cmd>]` launches the bash shell inside a Guest Container instead, and has a pre-condition: the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly. Both accept a single command to execute (`gshell ls -l`, `shell ifconfig`) and both are exited the usual way, for example with 'exit', returning to the CLI prompt.

No. `kill-session <session-id>` closes any established session regardless of type (CLI, NETCONF, etc), but the <session-id> supplied cannot match the id of your current session. To log yourself out you use the normal `exit` command instead. The session-id is a string in the form '<ip-address>:<port>' and must match an existing session; use `show session` to display the list of current sessions and get the correct id. Access Mode is Operational mode. Example: `kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212`.

Use the `message` command, which sends a message to other CLI sessions. Syntax: `message [message-content=]<value> [[target=]<value>]`. Access Mode is Operational mode. message-content is a string of 1-4096 characters. The target parameter selects the recipients and defaults to `all`; permitted values are `all` (all CLI sessions), `local` (only local sessions, serial console or CRAFT), `remote` (only remote sessions, e.g. SSH), a `session-id` (only that specific session), or a `username` (all CLI sessions of that user). Since the default is all, a plain broadcast is just `message "System will reboot in 5 minutes"`. To target one session: `message "System reboot in 5 minutes" 0.0.0.0:36`. The command can also be executed from NETCONF and RESTCONF, but the message is only ever delivered to CLI sessions.

The `property` commands set or show a type specific property that the system auto-instantiates but the user can configure. Syntax: `show property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value] [description]` and `set property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value <value>]`. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Two properties are supported. `fast-client-recovery` indicates whether fast client signal recovery is enabled or disabled in case of client signal failures; values are disabled or enabled, default disabled. `max-packet-length` indicates the maximum packet length supported by the CHM6 / CHM6L DCO; range 1518 to 18000, default 1518. The card-name is the name of the card the property applies to. Example: `set property-1-5/fast-client-recovery value enabled`.

Use `run`, which executes a previously configured/defined/scheduled task or a script. Syntax: `run task [[task-name=]<value>]` and `run script [-q] [-y] [-e=<value>] [-r] [[script-name=]<value>] [[arguments=]<value>]`. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Pre-condition: the task or script to be called must already be defined. task-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:scheduled-tasks/ioa-ne:task/ioa-ne:name; script-name is a relative path to the script directory, with optional arguments. Flags: -q runs the script in quiet mode (only command output shown, otherwise both the command and its output are shown), -r executes the script as a declarative config script, replacing system configuration with the script content, and -e sets the error option: continue (default), stop, or rollback. Examples: `run task collect-diag`, `run script config.cli -e=stop -q`.

They configure the same scheduled-command feature at different levels. `task` (add/set/show/delete task-<name>) is the user configurable scheduled task object, with attributes name (string 0..64), enabled (true/false, default true), label, alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), command (string 1..1024), command-type (cli, default cli), frequency (string 0..32 in the form '[xw][xd][xh][xm][xs]'), number-of-runs (no-limit or 1..65535, default no-limit), start-time, end-time (default never), persistent (default true), plus read-only task-status (scheduled/disabled/finished/ongoing), next-run, previous-run, previous-result (success/fail) and previous-output. `scheduled-task` is the container-level view of that same set of individual user-configurable scheduled commands: `add/set scheduled-task-<name> ...`, `show scheduled-tasks`, `delete scheduled-task-<name>`. Both are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Only if you are an SA user. `show session` lists the currently established management layer sessions, but only SA users can access the list of all sessions; all remaining users can see only their own session. Syntax: `show session-<session-id> [session-user] [session-type] [session-protocol] [created-time] [local-ip-address] [dial-out-server-name]`. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. session-id is the IP address and transport layer port number of the session, or 'NA' if the session was initiated from the serial port. session-type can be cli, snmp, netconf, restconf, webgui or gnmi; session-protocol can be telnet, telnet-raw, serial, ssh, ssh-raw, https or http. RESTCONF sessions appear in CLI if Cookie Based Authentication is used; the keep-alive defaults to 5 minutes and is changed with the restconf `cookie-timeout` attribute.

Yes. `set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...]` requires at least one attribute-value pair, and multiple pairs may be given as long as they belong to the same managed entity. You can affect several instances at once with the wildcard (*): as replacement of the whole instance key (card-*), of a single instance key (port-1-4-*; port-1-*-3), of all following keys to the right (odu-1-4,5,6,7-*), for auto-completing instance keys (user-admin*; ethernet-*), and for auto-completing attribute names (admin* instead of admin-state). Brackets give ranges (card-1-[1..4]) or lists (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]). Filters in the form <attribute>=<value> restrict the set to matching entities, e.g. `set port port-type=line admin-state lock`. The command asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances; -f forces it without confirmation and -v only validates. Access Mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

User access to the `shell` command can be limited to users in the NA, NE, and TT user-groups. The command runs in Operational Mode with syntax `shell [-h] [shell command]`. The shell is launched using the currently logged in user and allows only the commands accessible to that user, so privileges follow the CLI account. Certain commands and scripts can be launched with elevated privileges by prefixing them with 'sudo'; the possible sudo commands are /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient, and the /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts clear_downloads.sh, config_dns.sh, config_ip.sh, download.sh, install_os.sh, show_dns.sh, show_downloads.sh, show_ip.sh, show_route.sh, tunnelctl.sh, install_app.sh, remove_app.sh, CopyLogsToUSB.sh and docker.sh.

Yes. If a user executes a `show` command which generates more than 50000 objects, an error message is displayed to indicate that the output is too large. Narrow the request using an individual <entity-id> rather than a generic <entity-type>, or add filters (<attribute>=<value>) so only matching entities are displayed, or name specific attributes. The flags also help control volume: -c displays container instances only (no attributes), -a displays attributes only (no container instances), -x displays configuration/read-write attributes only, -o displays state/read-only attributes only, -t gives tabular format, -l long display, -d shows default values, and -r=<n> operates recursively for n levels down (full recursion if n is omitted). Piping to `more` displays long output page by page. Access Mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with `simulate`, which triggers simulated events in the system (alarms, equipment, etc). Syntax: `simulate [trigger=]<value> ([holder-AID=]<value> [type=]<value> [[subtype=]<value>] | [alarmed-entity=]<value> [alarm-type=]<value> [[alarm-direction=]<value>] [[alarm-location=]<value>])`. Access Mode is Operational mode. Triggers are raise-alarm, clear-alarm, plug-in-fru and plug-out-fru, though plug-out-fru is not supported. For equipment you supply the holder-AID (string 1..64) matching the card slot or tom port, plus the card type; subtype is optional (real hardware always has the subtype well defined). For alarms you supply alarmed-entity and alarm-type; if either is omitted when clearing, all simulated alarms are cleared. alarm-direction and alarm-location default to auto. The command works on a simulator and on a real system, but simulation cannot interfere with real HW, so you cannot simulate plugout of hardware that is physically present. Example: `simulate plug-in-fru 1-5`.

Yes. The `sleep` command specifies a delay for a specified amount of time, and the sleep time may be an arbitrary floating point number. Syntax: `sleep -h` and `sleep <time in seconds>`. The single parameter is the duration of the delay in seconds. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. `sleep 1` delays one second; `sleep 0.1` delays 100 milliseconds.

Add a task with no frequency set: leaving frequency empty makes it a single-occurrence task, and start-time is the timestamp at which it runs. Use `add task-<name> command <value> [enabled <value>] [label <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [command-type <value>] [frequency <value>] [number-of-runs <value>] [start-time <value>] [end-time <value>] [persistent <value>]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. command is a string of 1..1024 characters, command-type is cli (default cli), enabled defaults to true, alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited (default allowed), and persistent defaults to true so the task survives a system restart. The guide's own example: `add task-db_backup_once command "upload database file-server=xfr1" start-time 2021-04-23T05:05:00+00:00 alarm-report-control allowed label "DB Backup once"`. This requires the file server xfr1 to be configured beforehand. After it runs, task-status becomes finished and next-run becomes never.

`terminate` stops a running operation and runs in Operational Mode. Forms: `terminate location-led <entity>` (entity is a chassis or a card; ends a location led test started by `activate`, and has no effect if none is active), `terminate otdr [entity=]<value>` (stops an ongoing OTDR measurement on the given port), `terminate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<value>` (stops a manually triggered OTDR based Raman fiber check on an OTS-R entity; the scan is aborted abruptly, otdr ne function attributes and ots-r-auto-otdr auto-otdr-state revert to their prior state, and if that state was fail the PUMPS-DISABLED-OTDR-TEST-FAILED alarm is raised again; logs and available OTDR result files are saved), `terminate loopback [entity=]<value>[,<value>]*` (terminates WSS loopback on NMC entities; all channels under the loopback in a degree must be terminated and channels cannot be added or removed from an active loopback), and `terminate cable-id`. For CableID verification, the in-progress port-pair test runs to completion first, so the maximum delay is one port-pair verification time; confirm with `show cable-id cable-id-status` that cable-id-state has returned to idle.

`update` does not assign an arbitrary value the way `set` does; it triggers a predefined update action on an object attribute, determined by the <type> you provide. Syntax: `update [type=]<value> [[entity-id=]<value>[,<value>]*]`, Operational mode only (whereas `set` also works in Candidate Configuration mode). The permitted type values are: span-loss-alarm-threshold, which updates (re-evaluates) the OTS attribute span-loss-alarm-threshold; filter-insertion-date-now, which updates the chassis dust filter insertion date to the current date; set-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to under commissioning state, applicable to NEs entities in SLTE systems; and clear-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to Ready for Service state, also for SLTE NE entities. entity-id names the instance(s) to update and multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*). Examples: `update span-loss-alarm-threshold ots-1-1-dwdm-line`, `update filter-insertion-date-now chassis`.
